Climate change adaptation
The assessment of compliance with the climate change adaptation
(CCA) criterion for all EU Taxonomy-aligned activities of the
Latvenergo Group has been carried out in accordance with the
requirements set out in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU)
2021/2139, including Appendix A, which defines the criteria for

identifying, assessing, and managing material physical climate
risks across the lifecycle of assets and economic activities.
Climate risk management is integrated into the Group’s strategic
planning, risk management framework, and investment decisionmaking processes, ensuring alignment with the EU Taxonomy
requirement to avoid significant harm to climate resilience. While the
overall risk management framework addresses both transition and
physical climate risks, the CCA assessment specifically focuses on
physical climate risks, in line with EU Taxonomy requirements.
The assessment of physical climate risks is based on
internationally
recognised
methodologies
(including
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change AR6 and Task Force
on Climate-related Financial Disclosures recommendations),
regional climate projections developed by the Latvian Environment,
Geology and Meteorology Centre, the European Commission’s
climate hazard classification, and multiple climate scenarios
(SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0) across short-, medium-, and
long-term time horizons.
In line with Appendix A of the Commission Delegated Regulation
(EU) 2021/2139, the climate risk assessment covers hazard
identification, vulnerability analysis (including exposure, sensitivity,
and adaptive capacity), and the implementation of adaptation
measures addressing identified material risks.
For all Taxonomy-aligned activities, relevant acute risks (such as
storms, extreme precipitation, heatwaves, cold spells, and icing)
and chronic risks (including long-term changes in temperature,
wind patterns, precipitation regimes, and hydrological variability)
have been identified and assessed, taking into account the
geographic location, technical characteristics, and expected
operational lifetime of each asset.
Based on the assessment results, a set of climate adaptation
measures has been implemented, including infrastructure
resilience improvements, operational and business continuity
planning, real-time monitoring and early warning systems,
preventive maintenance and workforce preparedness, as well as
the integration of climate considerations into investment planning
and asset design. These measures are designed to reduce
vulnerability to identified climate hazards and ensure that
adaptation actions do not lead to maladaptation or increased
climate risks elsewhere.
The assessment indicates that no material unmitigated physical
climate risks have been identified for the assessed activities, and that
residual risks are managed at an acceptable level through the
implemented adaptation measures. The assessment is updated on a
regular basis and will be further expanded in the 2026 reporting period
to include supply chain impacts and long-term cumulative risks.

Not Taxonomy-aligned activities
4.29. Electricity generation from fossil gaseous fuels
Latvenergo Group operates electricity generation facilities fuelled
by fossil gaseous fuels (natural gas), which play an important role
in ensuring system reliability, balancing capacity and security of
supply in Latvia. These assets are used primarily to provide flexible
generation, reserve capacity and ancillary services to the
electricity system, supporting the stability of the transmission
network and the integration of variable renewable energy sources.
Electricity generation from fossil gaseous fuels does not meet the
EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria for a substantial
contribution to climate change mitigation under Activity 4.29.
Although modern gas-fired units operate with higher efficiency
and lower emissions than legacy fossil fuel technologies, they are
still based on fossil energy sources and therefore do not fulfil the
alignment criteria.
Replacement of fossil gaseous fuels with renewable or low-carbon
gaseous fuels is not currently feasible at scale for these units.
Latvenergo continues to monitor technological developments and
regulatory progress related to renewable and low-carbon gases.
All gas-fired generation facilities operate in compliance with strict
national environmental requirements and are covered by permits
for polluting activities, issued by the competent environmental
authorities. These permits regulate emissions to air, water and soil
and ensure that environmental impacts are appropriately managed.

4.30. High-efficiency co-generation of heat and power from
fossil gaseous fuels
Latvenergo Group operates high-efficiency cogeneration (CHP)
units fuelled by fossil gaseous fuels, supplying both electricity and
heat to customers, primarily in district heating systems. These
units improve overall fuel efficiency compared to separate heat
and power production and contribute to reduced emissions at
system level.
Despite their high efficiency, cogeneration from fossil gaseous
fuels does not meet the EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria
for substantial contribution under Activity 4.30. The use of fossil
fuels prevents classification as Taxonomy-aligned, even where
efficiency thresholds are achieved.
The CHP installations are operated in compliance with applicable
EU and national environmental legislation and are subject to
permits issued by the State Environmental Service, which include
enforceable emission limit values and operational conditions.
The assets continue to play a role in ensuring security of heat
supply and system flexibility, but until a transition to renewable or
low-carbon gaseous fuels becomes technically and economically
feasible, activity 4.30 is classified as EU Taxonomy not aligned.
4.31. Production of heat from fossil gaseous fuels in an efficient
district heating and cooling system
Latvenergo Group supplies heat generated from fossil gaseous
fuels within efficient district heating systems, as defined by
Directive 2012/27/EU. As such, the activity falls within the scope of
an EU Taxonomy-eligible economic activity under Activity 4.31.
However, heat production from fossil gaseous fuels does not meet
the EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria for alignment under
Activity 4.31, notwithstanding the efficiency of the district heating
system. Accordingly, Activity 4.31 is assessed as as EU Taxonomy
eligible but not aligned.
Heat production facilities are operated under valid environmental
permits and in compliance with applicable national and EU
requirements for emissions and environmental protection. These
assets remain necessary to ensure continuity and security of heat
supply, particularly during periods of high demand or limited
availability of renewable heat sources.

Accounting policies
Main principles, double counting and proxies
The calculation of financial metrics − revenue, CapEx, and OpEx −
has been performed in accordance with Taxonomy Regulation (EU)
2020/852, its delegated regulations and related documents. The
calculations are based on several assumptions described below. For
detailed indicator proportions, see the EU Taxonomy Tables section.
Taxonomy-eligible and Taxonomy-aligned KPIs are calculated as
the KPIs associated with each specific Taxonomy-eligible or
Taxonomy-aligned activity divided by Latvenergo Group’s total KPIs.
When determining the numerators, KPIs are allocated to Taxonomyeligible or Taxonomy-aligned activities based on the eligibility and
alignment assessment described in the previous sections.
It is assumed that any revenue, Taxonomy OpEx, or Taxonomy
CapEx that can be reliably attributed to an identified Taxonomyeligible or Taxonomy-aligned activity is classified accordingly.
Revenue and CapEx KPIs are directly linked to the ratios used in
the Latvenergo Group Consolidated and Latvenergo AS Annual
Report, while Taxonomy OpEx refer to the categories of operating
expenses defined under the Taxonomy Regulation.
For consolidated EU Taxonomy reporting, most consolidation
adjustments are applied in line with the principles used in the
Group’s consolidated financial statements.
All reported Taxonomy KPI financial figures are allocated directly
or, where necessary, split using appropriate proxies to the relevant
Taxonomy-eligible or Taxonomy-aligned activities, ensuring that
no double counting occurs. Latvenergo Group considers that all
Taxonomy-eligible activities contribute to climate change
mitigation; therefore, these activities are reported exclusively
under this environmental objective.
Where financial figures cannot be directly allocated to a specific
activity, the Group applies proportional allocation using the most
appropriate proxy based on the nature of the underlying activities.

Revenue

OpEx

The EU Taxonomy KPI on revenue has the same definition as Revenu
in Latvenergo Group Consolidated and Latvenergo AS Financial
Statements. The share of the Group’s Taxonomy-eligible and
Taxonomy-aligned revenue is calculated by dividing the revenue
generated from products or services associated with Taxonomyeligible or Taxonomy-aligned activities by the Group’s total revenue
(see Financial Statement section Statement of Profit or Loss).

Operating expenditures assessed for the purposes of the
Taxonomy disclosures include Latvenergo Group`s external raw
materials, repair, and maintenance costs (see Note No. 8 in the
section Financial Statements). The proportion of Taxonomy OpEx
for each Taxonomy activity is calculated as the share of OpEx
attributable to the respective Taxonomy activity relative to
Latvenergo’s total Taxonomy OpEx in 2025. The share of
taxonomy-eligible and aligned activities in OpEx are determined by
assessing the costs by operating segments, for example, for the
distribution service, as well as by analysing in detail the directly
attributable costs for other activities. In cases where expenses are
attributable by their nature to more than one of the types of
electricity and thermal energy generation listed in the taxonomy,
they have been reallocated in proportion to the amount of energy
generated in each of these activities. Cost allocation is carried out
in accordance with the established level of detail in financial
accounting, which enables the identification of costs attributable
to specific business segments.

The share of taxonomy-eligible and aligned activities in revenues is
based on an analysis of operating segments (e.g., the electricity
distribution segment) and product and service revenues (e.g.,
generation and trade of thermal energy, electric vehicle charging
services) that can be directly linked to specific Taxonomy operating
activities. Revenue associated with electricity generation includes
economic activities related to electricity generation from wind power,
hydropower, fossil gaseous fuels, solar photovoltaic technology,
cogeneration of heat and power from bioenergy, and the production
of heat and cooling from bioenergy. It also includes revenue generated
from infrastructure enabling low-carbon road transport and public
transport, as well as from the transmission and distribution of
electricity. Electricity supplied to customers is sourced both from
the Latvenergo Group’s power plants that meet the Taxonomy
requirements and from electricity procured on the market. Therefore,
Taxonomy eligible activities are attributed a proportional share of
total electricity sales revenue, corresponding to the share of
electricity generated by the Group’s power plants in relation to the
total volume of electricity sold, with the analysis performed on a
monthly basis.

The principles used for the allocation of revenue, CapEx and OpEx
ensure that these indicators are not allocated to several activities
in the taxonomy at the same time.
Changes in calculations
Compared to 2024, no changes were made to the accounting and
allocation principles for revenue and CapEx. However, in 2025 the
scope of OpEx included in the Taxonomy reporting was narrowed
to cover only external raw material, repair, and maintenance costs
(2024 – EUR 39.3 million ). In previous years, the Taxonomy OpEx
analysis included all Group`s operating expenses (2024 –
EUR 264.4 million). For comparability, the detailed Taxonomy
tables present data of 2024 aligned with the current approach.

Proportion of taxonomy-aligned activities

CapEx
The EU Taxonomy KPI on CapEx has the same definition as Capital
expenditure in Latvenergo Group Consolidated and Latvenergo AS
Financial Statements. The proportion of CapEx for each Taxonomy
activity is calculated as the share of CapEx attributable to the
respective Taxonomy activity relative to Latvenergo’s total CapEx
in 2025. CAapEx attributable to Taxonomy-eligible and
Taxonomy-aligned activities within total CapEx is determined
through a comprehensive assessment of all capital expenditure
made by the Latvenergo Group, analysed by operating segment
and at the level of individual CapEx projects.

• lower expenses in the electricity distribution segment, supported by a historically low number of
outages in the distribution network − the SAIDI and SAIFI indicators improved significantly, mainly
due to milder weather conditions

• lower overall electricity sales volumes (-366 GWh) and average sales prices, which impacted total revenue

• reduced maintenance and repair costs for CHPP assets

• lower electricity generation from HPPs (-266 GWh), resulting from less favourable hydrological conditions

• lower inventory‑related costs across other operating segments

Climate change adaptation
Impact of climate change on infrastructure resilience

LT

Latvenergo Group regularly assesses the risks caused by climate change and their impact on infrastructure, planning and
implementing resilience standards and protection solutions for infrastructure that ensure long-term adaptation and
resilience. Measures to improve infrastructure resilience are integrated into its strategic plans, also including climate risk
assessments in the planning of new projects. The Group works with regulatory bodies and follows international guidelines
to ensure compliance with best practices in climate resilience.

As part of the Green Deal, there are opportunities to LT
develop RES, storage solutions, the electric car
charging network, and new business ventures that
promote climate neutrality in the energy sector, related
industries, and society as a whole

In line with the Green Deal, Latvenergo Group:
• develops RES generation capacity in line with the goals set in the strategy
• expands the electric car charging network
• implements energy efficiency measures
• modernises and efficiently manages its distribution network, including the development of smart metering systems
• promotes cooperation with research institutions as part of conducting energy transformation and industrial research
projects

Decarbonization of the Group's generation portfolio, LT
ensuring sustainable and competitive operation of
generation assets

A plan to achieve climate neutrality for the Group’s combined heat and power plants was developed in 2024. In 2025,
individual technological solutions and their economic rationale were evaluated to ensure integration into the Group's
investment and development processes.

Development of new products and services, and MT
additional activities to develop the electric car charging
network

The development of new products and the improvement of existing ones ensure the Group’s competitiveness and
adaptation to market changes, contributing to its long-term growth. This enables the Group to expand into new niches
and meet growing consumer demand for innovation, quality and sustainability, while improving the efficiency and added
value of existing products.

Increase the energy efficiency of production and MT
business processes

The Group continuously improves the energy efficiency of its production facilities, infrastructure and buildings, also
making improvements in its monitoring and management systems and educating its employees and the public on topics
related to energy efficiency.

The Latvenergo Group Sustainability Strategy sets a number of GHG emission reduction targets, including achieving
climate neutrality in electricity generation by 2040 by developing RES generation and strengthening the efficient operation
of existing power plants. At the same time, improvements in distribution network quality are planned, along with the
development of electromobility and the electrification of the Group’s vehicle fleet, as well as a gradual shift in retail
towards more sustainable energy solutions.

A, OO,
P VC

The Group conducts a detailed analysis of GHG emissions in accordance with the ISO 14064-1 and GHG protocol
guidelines, in order to ensure accurate and responsible management of emissions and facilitate future reductions of these
emissions. The Group plans to work more closely with suppliers, foster sustainable purchasing practices, and support
solutions with lower GHG emissions across the value chain.

The availability of infrastructure connections, MT
necessary permit procedures and regulatory
constraints could affect the implementation of RES
projects

The availability of the necessary connections to the electricity power transmission grid can impede the integration of
renewable energy projects, affecting the ability of RES projects to deliver electricity efficiently and reliably. EIA
procedures can be time-consuming and cause delays or additional costs if unforeseen environmental issues are found.
Due to restrictions imposed by the Ministry of Defence, projects may be subject to additional restrictions in particularly
sensitive areas associated with national security or military operations. These restrictions can affect the location, design,
or operation of projects, potentially affecting project viability.

Fossil fuel-using assets in the generation portfolio can MT
make it difficult to raise external financing

Fossil fuel-based assets may not meet the sustainability requirements set by lenders, which can affect the amount, price
and other terms of available financing, making it more difficult to raise capital in the future.

Rising costs of renewable energy technologies can MT
delay the development of new projects or increase the
costs of their implementation

Higher costs can reduce the economic feasibility of projects. Investors and developers may face higher initial capital
requirements and longer return-on-investment periods. This can slow down the growth of the industry and delay the
transition to more sustainable energy sources.

The sections About the Group and Operating Segments provide
information on the geographical scope of Latvenergo Group’s
economic activities and its main operational sites. The Group
informs society about current policies, the impact of its activities
on climate change and the measures implemented to mitigate
these impacts by publishing information, including GHG emissions
data, on the Group’s website and preparing Sustainability
Statement and environmental reports, cooperating with
environmental
protection
institutions,
organizing
public
consultations on planned projects, and engaging in environmental
policy-making, thus promoting transparency and public
participation. This approach ensures open information flow and
promotes public involvement in climate change and environmental
protection-related issues.
Strategy resilience analysis scope
Latvenergo Group, as one of the leading participants in energy
sector in the Baltics, focuses on the development of renewable
energy, applies a comprehensive approach to assess and manage
both the transition and physical risks caused by climate change to
the Group's operations, as well as the Group's impact on the climate.
The risk management is integrated both in the strategy development
and implementation, as well as in operational activities.
The Group pays attention to essential aspects at key stages of the
value chain, starting from the procurement of raw materials and
resources, with sustainable procurement practices and suppliers
evaluation in terms of environmental criteria. In the context of the
main business, focus is placed on optimising production processes,
improving energy efficiency, and increasing the share of RES. In
the final stage of the value chain, the Group focuses on the
development of sustainable products and services, as well as
educating clients on energy efficiency and waste management in
line with circular economy principles. Information about risk
management at Latvenergo Group is available in the section
Internal Control System and Risk Management.
Climate impacts, risks and opportunities are included in the
Group's strategic approach. Transition risks and opportunities are
analysed and managed, taking into account economic, political,
technological and market factors and assessing physical climate
risks and their impact on the Group’s operations. As risks change
over time in response to socio-economic trends, environmental
processes and technological development, the identification and
implementation of risk mitigation measures must be flexible, up to
date and adapted to the impacts and consequences of changing
threats. Modern risk management is based not only on historical
experience, but also on forecasting future risks, monitoring and
adapting operational risk mitigation measures as well.

The transition risks arise from the global shift towards a low-carbon
economy and include factors such as new regulatory requirements,
technological innovations, market dynamics and changing consumer
preferences. Latvenergo Group mitigates these risks by purposefully
increasing RES capacities and aligning operations with the 1.5°C
climate target. Monitoring political and regulatory changes is essential
in long-term planning, and global trends are considered both in
strategic planning and in daily operations. The Group recognises that
the determining factors of transition risks may affect the viability of
certain business lines and create strategic risks without necessary
adjustments to business models in a timely manner.
The physical risks stem from the direct impacts of climate change
and encompass both acute events – such as extreme weather,
flooding, and heat and cold waves – and chronic changes, including
long-term shifts in temperature and wind patterns. The chronic risks
increase uncertainty in long-term energy genertion forecasts,
whereas acute risks may result in equipment downtime and increase
the scope of maintenance and repair activities across production
and infrastructure assets. The climate risk assessment is aligned
with the EU taxonomy principle of "do no significant harm" in the
field of climate change adaptation, while ensuring the necessary
protective measures and managing the associated operational risks.
The current resilience analysis focuses primarily on Latvenergo
Group’s own operations, as well as on its generation and distribution
assets. The upstream and downstream elements of the supply chain
were not included in the analysis for the time being. Also, the current
analysis does not include persistent physical risks after 2030,
indirect transition risks in the supply chain, and the cumulative longterm impact of risks. These limitations will be considered in the next
resilience analysis cycle. In the reporting year, the environmental
risk assessment methodology was revised to expand the scope of
analysis and ensure more comprehensive risk identification.
The low-carbon economy transition at Latvenergo Group is based on
a number of mutually related critical assumptions. The energy source
structure will gradually change as the share of renewables in the
electricity generation portfolio increases. This transformation will be
achieved through the combined use of the three main RES:
hydropower, solar and wind. The Group plans to increase the share of
renewable energy capacity in its generation portfolio to 80% by 2030.
The Group has set clear goals aligned with EU climate policy
scenarios: reduce GHG emissions by 47% by 2030 compared to 2021
levels, achieve climate neutrality in electricity generation by 2040, and
achieve full climate neutrality in all segments of operations by 2050.
The defined target applies to direct Scope 1 emissions arising from
processes and activities directly controlled by the Latvenergo Group.
The financial impact is managed by making targeted investments
in RES projects, reaching EUR 548 million in 2025. In order to

mitigate its risks, the Group is developing a diversified production
portfolio, focusing on RES. By 2026, the Group plans to install or
acquire WPPs and SPPs with a total capacity of 600 MW. After
2030, RES generation capacity is expected to increase to
2,300 MW. These investments are a part of the Group’s strategy
aimed at sustainable development and strengthening its
competitiveness on the regional energy market.
The goal of the physical climate risk assessment is to look at the
potential impact of climate risks on the Group’s operations and
make evidence-based decisions on climate change mitigation and
adaptation measures. Particular attention is paid to extreme
events/acute risks, identifying potential threats and opportunities
that could affect economic activity in the long run. Based on the
degree of the climate risk identified, decisions are taken on the
necessary adaptation measures, including their development,
financing, division of responsibilities, and deadline planning.
The Group initiated an assessment of physical climate risks and
resilience in 2023, in accordance with its environmental risk
assessment methodology. The analysis focused on extreme
weather events projected to undergo the most significant changes
and that could affect the continuity of the Group’s operations. The
first phase of the assessment covered HPPs, electric vehicle
charging infrastructure, as well as solar and wind power plants. In
2024, the resilience assessment was expanded to include support
processes and to evaluate the potential impact of climate risks on
the operation of CHPPs. The methodology provides for regular
reassessment of risks every three years, ensuring the continued
relevance of the analysis and the ability to respond in a timely
manner to evolving climate trends.
A resilience analysis based on the updated environmental risk
assessment methodology is under development at the time of
reporting. The analysis is based on Latvenergo Group’s Risk
Management Policy and is supplemented by a double materiality
assessment. These documents establish the fundamental
principles, while detailed analysis is conducted in accordance with
a separately developed methodology.
The Group considers how climate- and environment-related
events could affect operational continuity and how the nature of
its activities could increase reputational and/or liability risks. The
analysis of transition and physical risks has primarily been carried
out with a focus on the Group's own operations.
Resilience analysis methodology
Latvenergo Group ensures the regular updating of climate
information by comparing the Group's data and assumptions with
the latest IPCC assessment reports and other internationally
recognised climate change assessments.
112


=== pdf p.113 ===
Transition risks, including economic, business and geopolitical
risks, are managed in accordance with Latvenergo Group’s Risk
Management Policy. The responsibility for risk management is
allocated at different levels of the Group’s management, setting
clear duties and ensuring that risks are identified and managed in
line with its risk appetite. The Risk Management Policy is
supplemented by a double materiality assessment, used as an
assessment methodology and as a focused approach to solving
the issues of sustainability. New risks are regularly identified and
integrated into the overall risk management system, enabling a
prompt response to changes.
The 1.5 °C scenario was used to identify transition risks and
opportunities, in line with the EU 2050 climate neutrality goals, the
National Energy and Climate Goals and Latvenergo’s own
decarbonisation objectives. Within this scenario, the short-term
impact (up to 1 year) of changes in regulatory requirements (for the
entire asset portfolio), CO₂ quota price fluctuations (applies to the
CHPP-1 and CHPP-2), operational changes, and current
investment projects is analysed. In the mid-term (1–5 years),
attention is paid to technology modernisation needs, product
portfolio changes, market structure changes, and adaptations in
the asset portfolio, with particular emphasis on CHP facilities and
electricity grid infrastructure. The long-run assessment (more than
5 years) looks at fundamental changes in the business model,
strategic investments, the development of new business lines, and
the achievement of full decarbonisation. These considerations
apply across the entire asset portfolio and all operations of the
Group, as full decarbonisation targets entail a structural
transformation of the generation portfolio and the business model.

centrs VSIA, LVĢMC) has developed three climate scenarios
describing potential changes in air temperature, precipitation, wind
patterns, snow cover, sea level and coastal erosion.
The optimistic scenario (SSP1-2.6) foresees moderate climate
change with a global temperature increase of approximately 1.3–
2.4°C by the end of the century compared to the pre-industrial
period, if GHG emissions peak by approx. 2050 and then decrease.
The baseline scenario (SSP2-4.5) is characterised by moderate
climate change, where emissions continue to rise until the middle
of the century and then stabilise, while the global average
temperature may increase by 2.1–3.5°C by 2100.
The pessimistic scenario (SSP3-7.0) reflects significant climate
change, insufficient implementation of climate policies and further
increases in emissions, projecting a rise in the global average
temperature of 2.8–4.6°C by 2100. This scenario is used to assess
the maximum possible physical climate risks and the resilience of
the company's assets under various extreme conditions.
In risk planning, the baseline scenario (SSP2-4.5) is used as the
main reference scenario, while the pessimistic scenario (SSP37.0) serves as a resilience test under extreme conditions, allowing
for the assessment of the maximum possible impacts of climate
change. The optimistic scenario (SSP1-2.6) is used to test the
adequacy of planned adaptation measures in the event of less
pronounced climate change.

The Group has updated its environmental risk assessment
methodology and is currently developing a comprehensive climate
change risk profile. This includes an analysis of climatic factors
with a detailed assessment of climate change impacts and their
interactions, an in-depth analysis of local climatic trends, and a
structured risk assessment at the production and infrastructure
level, identifying the equipment and processes that are the most
sensitive to climatic changes.
The updated methodology is based on three sequential stages: (1)
initial operational review and identification of potential climate
risks; (2) detailed assessment of climate risks and vulnerabilities;
(3) evaluation of adaptation solutions for risk mitigation.
Climate risk assessment distinguishes between acute and chronic
risks. Acute risks (such as storms, extreme precipitation,
heatwaves) are analysed according to event intensity, frequency
of occurrence and potential immediate impact on infrastructure
and operational continuity. Chronic risks (temperature increase,
drought trends, long-term changes in precipitation patterns) are
assessed using a long-term scenario approach, identifying the
company's vulnerability and adaptive capacity under conditions of
prolonged change. Both approaches are complementary and form
a complete climate risk profile for the Group, covering both shortterm extreme events and gradual yet significant climate changes,
as well as their potential impact on the asset portfolio,
infrastructure and operational activities.

In the future, it is planned to expand the analysis with more detail
in the aspects of supply chain and downstream activities, and to
carry out an in-depth evaluation of assets in various transition
scenarios. Given that the updated version of Latvenergo AS
environmental risk assessment methodology was approved at the
beginning of 2026, the full integration of the aforementioned
aspects into the Sustainability Statement is planned for the 2026
reporting period.
The physical climate risk assessment is regularly updated, taking
into account internationally recognised climate change
assessment methodologies and the latest available scientific data,
including IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change)
guidelines. The assessment is updated in response to significant
changes in data or methodologies used, rather than at strictly
defined time intervals.
Based on the IPCC 6th Assessment Report (IPCC AR6, 2023) and
meteorological observation data, the Latvian Environment, Geology
and Meteorology Centre (Latvijas Vides, ģeoloģijas un meteoroloģijas
113


=== pdf p.114 ===
Latvenergo Group carries out a physical risk assessment of climate
change under the European Commission Delegated Regulation
(EU) 2021/2139 climate risk classification system using the
approach recommended by the TCFD (Task Force on Climaterelated Financial Disclosures). The analysis considers the latest
IPCC framework (IPCC AR6, 2023) and LVĢMC climate change
analysis tool scenarios, which are based on local meteorological
observation data (meteorological station data available to LVĢMC).
LVĢMC climate change forecasts are prepared for 30-year periods,
allowing for the identification of long-term climate change trends.
Climate hazards are analysed in emission scenarios SSP1-2.6,
SSP2-4.5 and SSP3-7.0 in three time perspectives: short term (up to
3 years), medium term (up to 10 years) and long term (up to 25 years).
It should be noted that LVĢMC projections currently do not include
a quantitative assessment of the differences in the frequency of
extreme events (such as heatwaves or intense precipitation)
between climate scenarios. Therefore, the analysis of acute risks
is carried out using a combined approach: LVĢMC general data on
changes in climate parameters are supplemented by international
research findings on changes in the frequency of extreme events
in various emission scenarios, as well as by expert assessments
based on historical event analysis and examples of industry best
practice.
In the risk assessment, three main components are analysed:
exposure (the exposure of assets and operations to climate
hazards), sensitivity (the susceptibility of company systems to
climate impacts) and adaptive capacity (the ability to adapt and
mitigate negative consequences). Together, these factors
determine the company's vulnerability to climate change. During
the assessment, the initial risk is first identified using a probability
and impact matrix, and then the residual risk is calculated,
considering the effectiveness of existing preventive and
adaptation measures. As a result, the company's level of climate
resilience is determined and further integrated into the Group's risk
management system, strategic planning and long-term
development programmes and also used in investment decisionmaking and priority setting.
The main objective of the assessment is to strengthen the climate
resilience of infrastructure and reduce the potential impact of
climate change on the Group's operational continuity and financial
results. Although data availability for the quantitative analysis of
acute risks is limited, the combined approach provides a sufficient
basis for risk level assessment and planning preventive measures.
With the introduction of the current version of the environmental
risk methodology in 2026, the Group will commence structured
monitoring of climate adaptation measures. For this purpose, a
monitoring report will be created, reflecting implementation

progress and key indicators by systematically compiling
information on planned activities, their baseline values and expected
changes until 2030, thus ensuring effective oversight of the
implementation of measures and evaluation of target achievement.
In addition, a detailed accounting mechanism for direct and indirect
losses, as well as preventive and adaptation measures in the context
of climate change, will be introduced, providing a structured
approach to both the analysis of historical losses (e.g. damage
caused by extreme weather events, operational interruptions,
reduction in production) and the assessment of future risks.
This approach enables the precise quantification of climate impact
costs, provides justification for the necessary investments in
protection and adaptation measures and identifies priority
investment directions. At the same time, it will strengthen the
Group's position in cooperation with investors and regulators,
providing clear justification for the necessity of climate resilience
measures and their economic efficiency.
The results of the resilience analysis confirm that all of the Group's
assets are structurally protected against the physical risks caused
by climate change. Protection is ensured by effective safety
measures and risk mitigation strategies, which are specifically
aimed at managing of acute physical risks. Considering the climate
scenarios and analysis results, no climate-related critical
assumptions have been identified that would significantly affect
the Group's financial results (see the Financial Statements section,
Notes to the Financial Statements No. 4. Significant accounting
estimates and judgements).
Latvenergo Group is aware of the materiality of climate change
risks and their gradual long-term development. It recognises that
these risks evolve gradually and can accumulate in the long run,
often materialising as rare events with severe consequences,
which in turn highlights the necessity to consistently improve
assessment methodologies in order to better understand climate
change processes and their potential impact on the Group’s
operations. Latvenergo Group’s risk management strategy also
includes maximum damage assessments that quantify potential
financial consequences and provides sufficient insurance
coverage against unforeseen extreme events.
The global renewables market continues to grow, and
considerable improvements in grid management, energy storage
solutions and the deployment of new technologies are expected in
the coming years. To adapt to these changes, Latvenergo Group
consistently monitors the market, by analysing political, legal,
technological, and market factors and their potential impact on the
Group’s operations and development outlook.
Climate change and environmental risks are properly managed by
ensuring appropriate and regular reporting to the management of

the Group’s capital companies. The Group has identified assets and
business activities requiring significant adaptation efforts, with
relevant information disclosed in the sections Transition plan and EU
Taxonomy. The Group does not engage in economic activities that
are incompatible with the transition to a climate-neutral economy.

E1-1

Transition plan
The Group is committed to achieving climate neutrality by 2050,
supporting the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming.
The Group’s transition strategy focuses on three main areas:
decarbonisation, development of RES, and improvements in
energy efficiency.
The approach to achieving the climate targets is based on
consistent work in the area of the environment, as evidenced by
regular progress monitoring and independent expert assessments.
The climate targets are integrated into the Group’s Sustainability
Strategy, approved at the end of 2023, adding specific
environmental, social, and governance objectives and targets in
the Medium-term Operational Strategy; see the section Group
Strategy. Latvenergo Group has set two important climate targets:
• in the medium term, the Group plans to reduce its direct GHG
emissions by 47% (compared to 2021) by 2030 while
increasing the share of RES in electricity generation to 80%
• in the long term, the Group has an ambitious goal of achieving
climate neutrality in electricity generation by 2040; in order to
attain it, active research is taking place in the area of CHPPs
decarbonisation solutions, with assessments of other
technological options to reduce emissions

Latvenergo plans to make substantial investments to achieve these
goals through the use of its internal resources as well as through
green financing and co-financing from EU funds. In setting its
strategic climate targets, Latvenergo Group conducted resilience
analysis to ensure its strategy and operations are adaptable to
economic, political, technological, and market factors associated
with the low-carbon transition, while also assessing physical climate

Latvenergo AS is the first company in the Baltics to have published

The Group consistently takes decarbonisation measures to
promote sustainable development and comply with climate change
mitigation requirements, while ensuring competitiveness on the
energy market. The Group’s strategy includes achieving its GHG
emission reduction targets and making significant changes in its
product and service portfolio, with a focus on sustainable solutions.
The strategic areas for decarbonisation are:
• expanding the use of RES – investments in new wind and solar
parks to increase renewable energy production
• efficiency improvements – modernisation and digitalisation of
production processes and infrastructure, aiming to reduce
energy losses and increase generating efficiency
• assessment and gradual implementation of economically
viable options for reducing fossil energy and decarbonising
production facilities
In the area of products and services, Latvenergo Group plans to
pursue technological modernisation:
• as part of the development of the electric car charging
infrastructure, it is expected that there will be build 1,200–1,500
charging ports in the Baltics by 2026 and 3,000 by 2030;

• in the area of smart solutions, there are developments in

• in developing the product and service portfolio, the focus is on
expanding the green energy offering; energy efficiency

emissions; investment projects are being developed in line with
the EU taxonomy regulations and climate neutrality targets
• decarbonisation of the value chain is realised in conjunction
with suppliers, in order to encourage the use of sustainable raw
materials and technologies
Latvenergo Group operates as a natural gas trader and uses
natural gas in its power generation facilities. Although the Group is
strategically moving towards decarbonisation and the
development of RES, there are currently locked-in emissions
associated with existing natural gas deliveries and the
infrastructure used. Locked-in emissions are future GHG
emissions resulting from already existing or planned infrastructure
and contractual obligations. In the case of Latvenergo, these arise
because the Group has long-term contracts for the supply of
certain quantities of natural gas, and because natural gas is used
to produce electricity and thermal energy at its CHPPs. Latvenergo’s
CHPPs play a critical role in the reliable and stable operation of
Latvia’s energy system, and there currently are no economically
viable alternatives available to replace natural gas. In order to reduce
the impact of locked-in emissions, Latvenergo continues to develop
its RES capacity, improve energy efficiency, and explore possible
decarbonisation technologies. Latvenergo Group knows that the
transition to climate-neutral energy is a strategic challenge and
continues to work on solutions that reduce GHG emissions while
ensuring a reliable and secure supply of energy.
Latvenergo Group has conducted a comprehensive analysis of its
GHG emissions. The assessment was carried out to ensure that
GHG emission reduction targets are met and to mitigate the
transition risks that may arise with changes in regulations and
market requirements.
Latvenergo Group faces a number of material transition risks that
affect its progress towards climate neutrality. The main financial
and technological risks encompass the substantial investments
necessary for deploying new RES technologies, upgrading existing
generation assets, and ensuring compliance with tightening
regulatory requirements. The rise in EU CO2 emission allowance
prices and the need to adapt to new market requirements could
have a substantial effect on the Group’s business operations.
However, several factors make achieving GHG emission reduction
targets difficult. Firstly, the dependence on fossil fuels and the
limited availability of stabilised decarbonisation technologies pose

challenges for the transition to climate-neutral solutions. Secondly,
geopolitical crises can cause short-term emissions increases, as
in 2022, when diesel fuel was used as backup. Thirdly, grid
infrastructure limitations hinder the shift to renewables, especially
with the planned increase in RES capacity in the long term. In
addition to these factors, emissions are expected to increase in the
coming years due to the more active operation of the CHPPs.
Following the synchronisation with the European power grid, the
CHPPs qualify for the balancing market, which enables them to
offer future service products on the balancing capacity market.
Protracted environmental impact assessment (EIA) procedures
also pose a major challenge, slowing down the implementation of
new projects. Administrative and regulatory challenges have a
substantial impact on the ability to meet set emission reduction
targets within the planned deadlines.
Latvenergo Group’s transition plan is integrated into its strategy and
financial planning. The plan focuses on Latvenergo’s transition to
sustainable operations, with the aim of reducing GHG emissions, thus
contributing to the Group’s compliance with the Paris Agreement and
sustainable development goals. This is supported by the 2022–2026
strategy goals and mechanisms for achieving them. There is an
ambitious growth programme envisaging an expansion of the
generation portfolio with RES projects across the entire Baltic region.
The transition is supported by certain financial instruments and
investment plans. In 2025, total investments reached
EUR 792 million, allocated for the development of new projects
and the modernisation of existing assets. More than two-thirds of
investments, EUR 548 million, was used for new wind and solar
generation capacities. Within implementation of the restructuring

E1-2

Policies
The key elements for managing climate change mitigation and
adaptation measures, as well as assessing risks and opportunities,
are included in the Latvenergo Group Medium-term Operational
Strategy for 2022–2026 and the Latvenergo Group Sustainability
Strategy for 2023–2026. For a summary of Latvenergo's policies
on climate change issues (IROs) management, see Policies
adopted to manage material sustainability matter in the section
General Information. In addition to the policies mentioned in the
section General Information and the third-party standards and
initiatives followed in their development, the Group’s approach to
sustainable development is based on its Environmental and Energy
Management Policy, which defines common principles, the
allocation of responsibilities, and requirements in the areas of
energy efficiency, efficient use of resources, and environmental
protection across the entire Group. The policy applies to all
companies within the Latvenergo Group and their organisational
units, as well as to activities within both the upstream and
downstream value chain, ensuring that environmental and energy
efficiency principles are integrated into procurement, infrastructure
maintenance, service delivery, and cooperation with external
partners. This policy is integrated into the Group’s strategy, and its
goal is to ensure sustainable business operations in line with national
and international environmental standards. It emphasises:
• moving towards climate neutrality

• implementing circular economy principles
• involving staff and the public in environmental affairs
• improving energy efficiency
• increasing the use of renewable energy sources
The policy was updated in 2025, aligning its structure and content
with ESRS requirements, integrating the double materiality
principle, clarifying the allocation of responsibilities and
strengthening a unified approach to the management of targets,
indicators and data. The update also broadens the perspective on
sustainability aspects in cooperation with partners, employees and
society, providing for regular and transparent communication and
stakeholder education and engagement in environmental and
energy management issues.
Information on the most senior level of management responsible
for the implementation of the policy, as well as a description of how
the interests of key stakeholders have been taken into account in
the policy development process, is provided in the section General
Information under Sustainability Management.

In addition to climate change mitigation activities, the Group
implements a climate resilience programme that includes
adaptation to the challenges of climate change. The adaptation to
climate change takes place in accordance with the Group’s risk
management policies. General information about risk management
at Latvenergo Group is available in the section Internal Control
System and Risk Management.
The risk management system is embedded in the Group’s risk
management policy, prescribing a uniform approach to identifying and
managing risks at all levels of governance. The climate risk
management process includes regular assessments of environmental
and climate risks, planning and implementing preventive measures,
and consistent monitoring of progress, coordinated by the
Environmental Management Function of Latvenergo AS in conjunction
with the responsible units of the Group’s companies.
At the same time, Latvenergo Group pursues a consistent energy
efficiency policy aimed at optimising energy consumption and
implemented in line with ISO 14001 and ISO 50001. The
implementation of the policy is coordinated by the responsible
units of the Group’s companies.

E1-3

Actions and resources
The Group takes consistent measures to reduce GHG emissions,
increase energy efficiency, and expand the use of RES. As part if
its climate change mitigation measures, the Group is investing in
renewable energy projects, improving production efficiency and
introducing low-carbon technological solutions that meet the
sustainability criteria set in the EU taxonomy. At the same time, the
adaptation strategy includes the modernisation of infrastructure
and management of climate risks to ensure a continuous and
reliable supply of energy in changing environmental conditions.

See the sections Group Strategy and Operating Segments for more
detailed information.
Climate change mitigation and adaptation measures cover the
Group's key value chain stages and stakeholders. In the upstream
value chain, suppliers’ compliance with environmental and climate
criteria is assessed, integrating sustainability requirements into
procurement processes and cooperation with supply partners (see
the section Policies). The Group's own operational value chain
stage includes infrastructure climate resilience and mitigating
potential climate change impacts to ensure business continuity, as
well as employee protection measures during extreme weather
conditions. For employee protection, safety instructions have been
developed, and the necessary personal protective equipment has
been provided. Regular training on emergency procedures is
organised to ensure safe and uninterrupted operational activities.
Accordingly, the Group has implemented several support and
compensation mechanisms in the downstream value chain. As part
of the client assistance programme, consultations on improving
energy efficiency are provided, offering solutions for optimising
electricity costs. The Group regularly informs customers about
energy efficiency measures as well as broader environmental and
sustainability issues, promoting more mindful electricity
consumption. These activities support changes in customers’
awareness and consumption habits, strengthening the importance
of energy efficiency and creating preconditions for an increasing
number of customers to choose electricity generated from
renewable energy sources in their electricity consumption. 54
In the field of adaptation of infrastructure, the modernisation of
power grids was carried out, smart technologies were implemented,
and preventive measures were taken to protect critical infrastructure
against extreme weather events. Particular attention is paid to the
safe operation of HPPs and the efficient management of water
resources in the Daugava River Basin. The Group continues the
development of the Plavinas HPP back-up spillway project in order
to increase the reliability of the HPP and the energy security of the
country. The purpose of the back-up spillway is to provide an
additional water throughput capacity of at least 4,000 m3/s, in order
to reduce the risk of the dam breaking and to divert flood water. The
measures resulted in better reliability of supply, reducing the number
of unscheduled power interruptions.
The Group proactively manages its material climate-related IROs in
order to prevent or mitigate negative impacts on the environment
and society, prevent potential harm to third parties, and reduce
future risks associated with climate change. Within the Latvenergo
Group, management systems and procedures have been

In the reporting year, two BESS projects with a total capacity of 10.6

capacity of 183.4 MW / 428.6 MWh are in the development stage.
In the reporting year, 3.1 TWh of electricity generated from RES
resulted in CO₂ emission savings of 1,577 thousand tonnes. This
calculation is based on the residual mix emission factor for electricity
(AIB: European Residual Mixes 2024 (2025)) and reflects the amount
of emissions that would have been generated if the corresponding
volume of electricity had been produced using fossil energy sources.

Investments in modernising infrastructure – investments in
distribution reached EUR 172 million, which is about one-fifth of the
Group’s total investments (see the section EU Taxonomy). About
25% of the distribution segment’s funds are invested in the
construction and reconstruction of power lines and transformers,
thereby ensuring high-quality network services, technical
performance, and operational safety. EU funding is also being
attracted for the modernization of the electricity distribution
system within the framework of the Recovery and Resilience
Facility, implementing two projects with total funding of nearly EUR
102 million during the period from 2023 to 2026. The purpose of
investments in the distribution segment is to increase the reliability
and resilience of the electricity distribution network, reduce the
frequency and duration of planned and unplanned power outages,
improve voltage quality, and at the same time strengthen the
network’s readiness for growing demand and the integration of
renewable energy sources.
Fostering electromobility – at the end of 2025 the number of
charging ports installed at Elektrum Drive charging stations
increased to 1,107. By using the e-mobi network in Latvia and at
LIDL charging stations in Lithuania and Estonia Elektrum Drive
customers had access to a total of 1,590 charging ports in the
Baltics. In 2025, approximately 195 thousand electric vehicle
charges were made, comprising 4,150 MWh, resulting in savings
of more than 2,360 tonnes of CO2 emissions.
During the reporting year, the heat storage system at CHPP-2
made it possible to store cogenerated heat and better adapt the
operating modes of the CHPP to market conditions and to covering
peak loads, resulting in efficient consumption of energy and
5.1 thousand tonnes of CO2 emission savings.
In addition to technological solutions, Latvenergo Group
implemented nature-based climate change mitigation measures:
tree planting initiatives were implemented in conjunction with local
partners to increase carbon capture potential.
The costs and investments associated with the above activities are
shown in the activity costs, capital investments, and capital investment
plan, as per the taxonomy (see the section EU Taxonomy). Latvenergo
Group has set itself a goal of continuing to make at least 80% of its
investments in EU taxonomy-aligned activities.
E1-4

Targets
Latvenergo Group has set specific GHG emission reduction targets
to manage material climate-related IROs. The Group calculates
GHG emissions for carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous

oxide (N₂O), and fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-gases). All
emission amounts are expressed in tonnes of carbon dioxide
equivalent in order to standardise the impact of different gases,
taking into account the global warming potential of each gas. This
approach ensures comparability and transparency of emission
data, as well as its effective use in setting climate targets and
planning emission reduction measures.
The year 2022 was selected as the baseline year, aligning with the
period of the Latvenergo Group’s Medium-term Operational
Strategy for 2022–2026. An exception applies to Scope 1 GHG
emissions, for which the baseline year is set at 2021. Due to the
geopolitical situation and the unusual operation of generation
facilities in 2022 (such as the use of diesel fuel as a backup in
CHPP boilers) the emissions data from that year do not objectively
reflect a reliable reference point for setting emissions targets.
The Group has set targets in the areas of climate change mitigation,
energy, and climate changeadaptation:
• in order to mitigate climate change, the Group aims to reduce
Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions
• the energy industry is the Group's core business, and the
Group's 2022–2026 business strategy sets ambitious
decarbonisation targets, including the development of new
RES generation capacity and the modernisation of the power
distribution grid in line with microgeneration and electrification
trends (see the section Group strategy)
• in terms of adaptation to climate change, the Group is focused
on efficient management of the power grid, improving the
reliability and quality of power supply, including strengthening
grid resilience to the impacts of climate change (see the
section Distribution)
The main long-term objective is to achieve climate neutrality by
2050, with an interim target to reduce direct GHG emissions by
47% (i.e., 441.8 thousand tonnes of CO₂e) by 2030, including a
reduction of the specific emission intensity per MWh of electricity
generated to 0.06 tonnes CO₂e compared to the 2021 baseline
level. The defined target applies to direct Scope 1 emissions
arising from processes and activities directly controlled by the
Latvenergo Group. These emissions are the most precisely
measurable and manageable, enabling the establishment of clear,
results-oriented reduction targets.
The Group has not set an absolute or specific reduction target for
total Scope 2 GHG emissions. The majority of these emissions are
associated with electricity losses in the distribution network,
which cannot be fully eliminated for technological reasons.

118


=== pdf p.119 ===
Given the increasing electricity consumption and distribution volumes, the Group maintains electricity
network losses at a stable level through operational and technological measures, while recognizing
that as grid load increases, the technical challenge of preventing a rise in loss intensity also increases.
However, in order to reduce their impact, the Group sets targets to limit electricity losses and to
increase the share of certified renewable electricity in its own consumption.
Indirect Scope 3 emissions, which occur outside the Group’s direct operational control, are more
complex to measure accurately and to influence directly. No targets have been set for reducing total
absolute and specific Scope 3 emissions; however, the Group has defined measures to mitigate these
emissions, including the gradual reduction of emissions from electricity retail activities and the
promotion of customers’ selection of renewable electricity. A detailed description of the alignment
between the targets and the objectives set out in the policies is provided in the section Policies.
Results achieved in 2025:
• direct (Scope 1) emissions fell by 17% compared to 2021 during the reporting year. The specific
emissions rate was 0.100 tonnes of CO2 per megawatt-hour (MWh) of electricity generated
• electricity generated from RES accounted for 66% of the total electricity output
• the share of electric vehicles in Latvenergo Group's fleet increased to 15.6%
• the share of certified electricity in the Group's total consumption was 80%
• electricity distribution losses amounted to 3.66%
• emissions from electricity retail trade increased by 8% compared to 2022. Although the share of
green electricity chosen by customers in 2025 remained similar to that in 2022, the 2025 emission
factor for uncertified electricity was significantly higher than in 2022. Consequently, each kilowatthour of uncertified electricity sold generated more emissions than in the 2022 reporting period
• 12% of retail electricity clients chose green energy
The GHG emissions reduction target indicators were developed with consideration of the EU Green
Deal goals and the 2021–2030 Latvian National Energy and Climate Plan into account. The target
indicators were set based on the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Net Zero Emissions by 2050
scenario and the energy sector decarbonisation roadmap. To ensure that the targets are aligned with
the actual emissions situation, an initial assessment of the Group’s GHG emissions inventory data was
carried out during the target-setting process, analysing the emissions structure, the main emission
sources, and historical trends. Based on this assessment, the targets were defined, ensuring
consistency with the GHG emissions inventory boundaries, methodology, and underlying data.
In 2024, Latvenergo AS received an NZ-3 score from Moody’s, which analyses the compliance of the
Group’s climate transition strategy and goals with global efforts to limit warming to 1.5 °C. The Moody’s
assessment is science-based, as it follows internationally accepted IPCC climate science findings and
scenarios. The methodology used by Moody’s integrates the latest IPCC climate models, permissible
emissions calculations and sector decarbonisation trajectories, ensuring that the rating represents the
most up-to-date scientific knowledge on climate change. Moody’s assesses not only the
ambitiousness of the goals but also their consistency with science-based decarbonisation strategies and
realistic implementation opportunities, enabling a science-based approach to evaluating climate goals.
The target indicators were set with consideration of future development factors, including anticipated
changes in sales, shifts in consumer habits and needs, regulatory requirements, and planned
technological solutions.
For information on plans to introduce new technologies and their role in achieving GHG emissions
reduction targets, see the sections Transition plan and Group Strategy.

E1-5

Energy consumption and mix
Total energy consumption in the reporting year decreased by 2%
compared to 2024. Fossil fuels accounted for 91% of energy
consumption, while renewables accounted for 8%. The share of
uncertified electricity from nuclear sources was 0.9% of the total
energy consumption.
Energy consumption and its breakdown were calculated and
grouped according to ESRS requirements, which may cause
differences compared to reports from previous years, in which
calculations were made using other standards. Energy
consumption includes direct and indirect energy consumption.
Direct energy consumption covers all forms of energy use,
including those that contribute to Scope 1 GHG emissions. This
includes all fuels used in the Group’s combined heat and power
plants and boiler houses, as well as other energy sources: petrol
and diesel fuel. Indirect energy consumption consists of the
Group’s heat and electricity consumption.

E1-6

GHG emissions
The assessment of Latvenergo Group’s GHG emissions was
conducted in accordance with the requirements of ISO 14064-1
and the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting
Standard. The operational control approach was chosen for
assessing Latvenergo Group’s GHG emissions. The approach
considers GHG emissions from activities over which the
organisation has operational control, meaning the organization can
make decisions and implement policies that directly address
emission sources and their management. In the assessment
process, no external tools are used. All GHG emissions are
expressed in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (t CO2e) in order
to standardise the impact of these gases, taking the global
warming potential of each gas into account. This approach allows
for the standardization of the impact of different GHGs (CO2, CH4,
N2O, HFC, SF6), converting them into a single unit for easier
comparison and more effective emissions management. The
Group’s GHG emissions data for all scopes have been verified by
an independent third party, Bureau Veritas Latvia SIA, confirming
the compliance of the emissions calculations with applicable
standard requirements and the reliability of the data.
Direct (Scope 1) GHG emissions and their intensity
Direct, or Scope 1, GHG emissions include emissions from sources
owned or controlled by the Group. The amount and intensity of these
emissions at Latvenergo Group are influenced by the share of RES in
primary energy consumption, the volume of energy generated, and
the operating regimes of generation facilities.
GHG emission intensity is expressed in tonnes of carbon dioxide
equivalent and is measured per unit of electricity (MWh) generated
by the Group. The lower this indicator, the higher the share of
electricity generated from RES and the more efficiently the CHPPs
have operated.
Scope 1 emissions at the Group mainly arise from fuel combustion
plants (i.e., combustion plants with a nominal thermal input above
20 MW), which participate in the EU Emissions Trading System
(ETS). However, a small share (0.6%) of emissions from
combustion plants originates from units not included in the ETS.

Scope 2 emissions are calculated by multiplying the amount of
energy purchased by the respective emission factors. Scope 2
emissions are calculated according to the GHG protocol, using the
location-based and market-based methods.

*Source: European Environment Agency (2024)

In 2025, fuel consumption by vehicles and machinery resulted in
7.3 thousand tonnes of CO₂ emissions. The Group operates
facilities using fluorinated GHG gases, the leakage of which in the
reporting year resulted in emissions equivalent to 0.2 thousand
tonnes of CO₂. Expanding the boundaries of emission calculations,
the 2025 assessment also includes emissions from HPP reservoirs.
The main contributor in this context is methane (CH₄) emissions,
which are generated under anaerobic conditions, i.e., in the
absence of oxygen, in sediments and flooded organic matter.
Direct GHG emissions from heat and power plants are calculated based
on the amount of fuel used, in accordance with EU ETS requirements.
Other direct emissions are calculated by multiplying relevant activity
data by the corresponding emission factors. The assessment of
emissions from HPP reservoirs is based on their surface area data and
emission factors defined in international guidelines.
Compared with 2024, total direct GHG emissions decreased by 2%,
while the emission intensity per MWh of electricity generated
increased, as total electricity generation decreased by 3%, while
electricity generation from CHPPs increased by 2%.
Indirect (Scope 2) GHG emissions
Indirect Scope 2 GHG emissions are emissions generated as part
of the production of electricity and heating energy consumed by
the Group and purchased from other producers. Latvenergo Group
not only generates energy but also consumes heat and electricity
as part of maintaining its production and administrative buildings.
The heating energy and electric power are purchased from various
suppliers, and in order to determine the corresponding emissions,
the Group’s own heat and electricity consumption records are used,
as well as supplier-provided data and publicly available reports.

When assessing Scope 2 emissions using the location‑based
method, it can be concluded that the emissions intensity of
electricity supply networks in Lithuania and Estonia decreased,
supported by a higher share of electricity generation from RES. In
contrast, emissions intensity in Latvia increased slightly due to a
higher share of electricity generation from fossil energy sources.
Overall, total emissions calculated according to the location‑based
method increased by approximately 24%.
Under the market‑based method, total Scope 2 emissions
decreased by approximately 4%, which is explained by a reduction
in the emissions intensity of the Residual Mix of non-certified
electricity. The Residual Mix represents the average emissions
intensity of electricity remaining in the grid after deducting
electricity covered by issued and cancelled guarantees of origin.
In the reporting year, 80% of the Group’s electricity consumption
was covered by guarantees of origin. Together with a reduction in
energy consumption, this contributed to a decrease in Scope 2
emissions under the market‑based method, even though the
location‑based method indicates an increase in emissions.
Indirect (Scope 3) GHG emissions
Scope 3 GHG emissions are other indirect emissions, generated as
a result of Latvenergo’s activities: through supply chains and the
use of the Group’s products and services. While the 2023 annual
report included four categories of emissions in its Scope 3
calculation, the 2024 annual report already takes account of all
significant Scope 3 emissions related to the Group’s activities, with
improvements in the emissions assessment methodology and an
update on the amount of Scope 3 emissions in 2023. Scope 3 GHG
emissions are calculated using emission factors that describe the
ratio of the quantity of a pollutant to an activity-specific parameter
associated with GHG emissions.
Emissions are not assessed for the categories Processing and
handling of products sold (Category 10), Franchises (Category 14),
or Investments (Category 15). The operations of Latvenergo Group
companies are not associated with activities in these categories.
To date, no specific estimates have been made regarding the
share of primary data in emissions calculations.
121


=== pdf p.122 ===
The majority of Scope 3 GHG emissions are calculated using
secondary data, with emissions determined based on
internationally recognized emissions factor databases as well as
national emissions factors. The company plans to increase the
proportion of primary data in future reporting periods as part of its
ongoing efforts to improve GHG emissions tracking.

reflect the average emission intensity of the respective sectors.

to the delivery of the product or service, including raw material
extraction, production, and transportation. Life cycle emissions
related to specific energy generation and infrastructure assets are
included indirectly; however, detailed life cycle assessments at the
level of individual assets or projects are not performed. Therefore,
the results reflect industry-average indicators rather than the
specific impacts of individual technologies or suppliers.

The largest share of emissions within this category is attributable
to construction works, as well as the purchase of electrical
equipment and other machinery and equipment. Construction
works primarily cover energy infrastructure development projects,
as well as maintenance, reconstruction, and repair activities
associated with both investment project implementation and dayto-day operations. Meanwhile, the categories of electrical
equipment and other machinery include the acquisition,
replacement, and maintenance of technological equipment,

machinery, and systems required for the implementation of new
projects and the continuous operation of existing infrastructure.
Emissions in Category 5 increased significantly in 2025, reaching
1,668 t CO₂e, representing a 257% increase compared to 2024.
This increase was driven by the remediation of the CHPP‑2
technological sludge storage facility, which was initiated in 2024
and fully implemented during the reporting period. The project
involved the removal of historical sludge and other waste to

mitigate potential contamination risks associated with the historical
use of heavy fuel oil as a fuel source. These wastes accounted for
the majority of the increase in emissions within this category. As
this type of waste is no longer generated as a result of the Group’s
operations and the remediation project has been completed, no
further emissions of this magnitude under the Category 5 are
expected in future years.

Latvenergo Group’s GHG emissions by scope

124


=== pdf p.125 ===
The emissions factors used for calculating the Group’s GHG
emissions were selected based on the priority approach outlined
in the GHG Protocol guidelines. National emissions factors were
applied wherever available, as they provide the highest accuracy
in reflecting the specific characteristics of the relevant
geographical location and sector. In cases where national
emissions factors were unavailable, internationally recognized
sources, such as DEFRA emissions factors, were used, as they are
widely accepted in global GHG reporting practices. Additionally, to
calculate indirect (Scope 3) emissions, the EXIOBASE database
was used, offering detailed emissions factors across various
sectors and countries, enabling the assessment of supply chain
emissions in different geographical areas and economic sectors.
E1-7
Projects financed through carbon credits
Latvenergo Group does not currently use GHG capture and storage
technologies in its operations. The Group did not buy any carbon
credits to reduce or capture GHG emissions. The Group continues
to monitor climate change-related regulatory and market
developments and will, if necessary, assess the potential for
developing respective initiatives in the future.
E1-8
Internal carbon pricing
The Group currently does not use internal carbon pricing schemes.
However, given the tightening of climate policy regulation and
market trends, the Group plans to assess the possibility of
introducing such schemes in the future. The assessment process
will involve an analysis of how internal carbon pricing could
support decisionmaking and contribute to the implementation of
the Group's climate related action policies and targets.

E1-9
Anticipated financial effects of material physical risks
Latvenergo Group is aware of the materiality of climate change
risks and their gradual long-term development. These risks often
materialise as rare events with severe consequences, highlighting
the need for the continuous improvement of assessment
methodologies. This enables a better understanding of climate
change processes and their possible impact on the Group ’ s
operations. Latvenergo's risk management strategy includes
maximum damage assessments that quantify potential financial
consequences and provides sufficient insurance coverage against
unforeseen extreme events. Climate change threatens both the
stability of production capacity and the reliability of infrastructure,
causing additional unpredictability in the Group’s operations and
financial flows.
A full reassessment of physical climate risks is planned for 2026 in
line with the regular three-year reassessment cycle; as part of this,
the potential financial impact of the identified risks will also be
evaluated.
Anticipated financial effects of material transition risks
The effect of transition risks on Latvenergo Group is determined
by a number of mutually related factors, including regulatory
changes, market trends and technological innovation. The rise in
the price of carbon puts substantial financial pressure on the
Group, as the rise in the price of CO2 emission allowances
increases its costs, especially in areas where fossil fuels are still
used. At the same time, tightening requirements in renewable
energy and decreasing subsidies on the energy market call for
substantial additional investment in low-carbon generation
capacity, which could lead to mid-term cash flow instability and
affect financial results.

The availability of power transmission network connections, the
complexity of EIA procedures and the restrictions imposed can
impede the implementation of renewable energy projects, which
can slow down project development and considerably increase
costs.
Potential to benefit from climate change-related Opportunities
Latvenergo Group faces a broad range of strategic opportunities
in the context of energy transition and climate policy development,
which can provide substantial long-term financial benefits. The
planned investments in solar and wind projects up to 2030 can
significantly increase green energy generation capacity, providing
stable income streams that are less dependent on fluctuating fossil
fuel prices and the cost of CO2 emission allowances. Following the
priorities of the European Green Deal, Latvenergo continues to
develop renewable and other climate-neutral energy sources,
something that is already being implemented as part of its midterm
and sustainability strategies. Active development of new
production capacities enables the Group to strengthen its position
on the regional energy market and reduce its dependence on
imported energy.
Latvenergo has the potential to become a central player in the
Baltic region's energy transition, taking advantage of its expertise
in hydropower, innovative approaches to the development of
renewable energy, and its regional presence. The Group’s strong
financial position makes it possible for it to implement large-scale
investment projects that contribute to sustainable growth and the
development of new business areas. Overall, Latvenergo can not
only adapt to the challenges caused by climate change but also
actively use the transformation of the energy sector to gain
longterm financial benefits.

The growing sustainability expectations among consumers and
investors have a substantial impact on lending terms and on the
cost of raising investment. Stricter environmental, social, and
governance (ESG) criteria and compliance with EU taxonomy
requirements will become decisive factors in future financial
planning and the raising of capital. Latvenergo faces a double
challenge: on the one hand, it needs to reduce emissions and the
costs associated with them; on the other, it has to provide
substantial investment in green energy projects to remain
competitive and compliant with regulations in the long run.
Furthermore, changes in consumer behaviour leading towards
more environmentally friendly products and services can create
both new business opportunities and additional pressures to adapt
the business models.
