=== pdf p.138 ===
Latvenergo Group’s policy on deforestation is grounded in a
systematic approach to compensating for deforested areas, which
includes afforesting equivalent areas and developing renewable
energy projects while preserving biodiversity.
The development of wind farms in forest areas is assessed in areas
which Latvijas valsts meži AS (Latvian State Forests) has identified
as potentially suitable for detailed nature expert studies and
environmental impact assessment based on the criteria set out in
regulatory enactments and analysis of available data. In such areas,
optimisation is carried out by combining several functions and
ensuring efficient and multifunctional land use in cooperation with
certified nature experts and the Nature Protection Board. To ensure
environmental sustainability and reduce the potential negative
impact on biodiversity, the Group involves industry specialists and
conducts research on the suitability of innovative technological
solutions for wind farm operation, including solutions that improve
the protection of birds and bats or reduce risks to other species. The
Group establishes strategic partnerships with Latvijas valsts meži AS
to ensure sustainable management of the forest resources and
responsible management of the areas. At the same time,
professional environmental experts carry out environmental impact
assessments, ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements
and internationally recognised best practices. Cooperation with
ornithologists and other nature protection specialists ensures that
the planning and development of wind farms comply with mandatory
environmental protection requirements and are implemented under
species and biotope protection requirements.
E4-3

Actions and resources
Latvenergo actively pursues a biodiversity conservation and
restoration strategy focusing on long-term ecosystem protection
and sustainable management, which mainly includes:
• monitoring measures – regular surveillance of biodiversity and
the status of ecosystems; monitoring fish populations and
spawning grounds in the Daugava River basin is particularly
important, as is monitoring birds and bats in wind farm areas.
Monitoring is carried out annually, ensuring continuous data
collection and long-term impact assessment
• restoration work – river cleaning and restoration projects in the
Daugava River basin, artificial fish restocking, afforestation.
Activities are planned in the short term (annually), medium term,
and long term to ensure strategic and systematic ecosystem
restoration

• nature conservation measures and biodiversity awareness –
personnel training, educational events for the public,
information materials and live broadcasts from nature
observation sites. These activities are implemented
periodically to promote long-term impacts on biodiversity
The biodiversity measures implemented and planned by the
Latvenergo Group primarily relate to own operations, while also
covering certain parts of the upstream value chain and ecosystem
and societal initiatives implemented within the downstream value
chain.
Activities related to managing ecosystems in the Daugava River
basin
HPPs affect adjacent habitats, river ecosystems and fish migration.
To mitigate these impacts, Latvenergo consistently adheres to the
requirements of the water resource use permits issued to HPPs
regarding minimum and maximum water level limits, level drop
speed during operation and other operational restrictions,
including restrictions during periods of massive fish spawning. To
manage the ecosystems of the Daugava River basin, the Group has
developed the 'Action Plan for Migration and Natural Reproduction
of Anadromous Fish of the Daugava River Basin 2021–2025.' The
plan outlines regular placement of artificial fish spawning nests in
reservoirs, river cleaning projects within the Daugava River basin,
scientific research to support fish migration, monitoring, and
impact assessments. The Biodiversity Transition Plan
complements this approach by defining specific actions and
activities to mitigate the impact of hydropower plant operations. It
aims to continue and improve existing practices in managing of the
Daugava River basin ecosystems and, if necessary, to implement
additional measures during its operational period from 2026 to
2028, in order to strengthen ecosystem protection and sustainable
management of water resources.
Activities related to managing of the impacts of wind and solar
parks
During the development of new renewable energy projects,
comprehensive EIAs are conducted, and innovative yet
economically viable solutions for biodiversity preservation are
sought. During the project development stage, an initial
environmental risk and impact assessment or equivalent is carried
out for all wind and solar park projects to assess the potential
impact on biodiversity and ecosystems at the locations of potential
new facilities. Impact assessment processes stipulated by laws
and regulations are implemented to provide information on
biodiversity and ecosystems in the respective area. Action plans

to mitigate potential impacts and identify restoration measures are
developed on the basis of the environmental impact assessments.
To reduce risks, detailed EIAs are performed prior to the
construction of wind farms. They are designed to assess the
impact on landscapes, habitats, birds and other species, as well as
other factors. To minimise potential negative impacts, the process
of wind farm development includes designing state-of-the-art
technologies, such as camera systems to monitor bird migrations
and automatic turbine shutdown mechanisms, as well as best
practices with respect to wind farm location and design.
Recognising the importance of ornithological research and bird
conservation measures, Latvenergo AS has established a
permanent position for an ornithologist. In the reporting year, the
Group continued its study on the potential cumulative impact of
wind farms developed in forest areas on the black stork population
in Latvia, launched in cooperation with the University of Latvia in
2024.
In the reporting year, Latvenergo Group continued the
development of solar parks, following the guidelines developed in
2024, in the creation of which the Group participated. The main
objective of these guidelines is to promote sustainable and
efficient development of solar park projects while preserving
nature
and
the
landscape.
The
guidelines
include
recommendations on balancing nature conservation, public
interest and economic benefits at all stages of solar park
development – from site selection to decommissioning – with an
emphasis on responsible construction, management and
maintenance practices. When developing solar parks, Latvenergo
follows the recommendations provided in the guidelines and, on its
own initiative, makes additional improvements to solar parks that
supplement the mandatory requirements of environmental
protection regulations.
Electricity distribution line route management
Construction and maintenance of electricity power lines requires
the clearing of land and creation of travel routes, which can have
negative impacts on local ecosystems, especially when the work
is carried out in areas with high biodiversity. To mitigate these risks,
Sadales tīkls AS implements a number of measures:
• tailored planning – construction of the routes is planned taking
into account the local ecosystem and its conservation needs to
minimise biodiversity loss and avoid impacts on protected
habitats and species; existing infrastructure corridors are used
where possible to minimise additional impacts on the natural
environment

138


=== pdf p.139 ===
• protection of trees and vegetation – selective tree felling
methods are used for the clearing and maintenance of routes
to prevent excessive tree felling and habitat damage, and less
invasive methods are used to maintain vegetation, for instance,
mowing, to help conserve lowland habitats and populations of
pollinators
• soil and water protection – construction and maintenance work
on transmission lines is organised in a manner that reduces the
risk of pollution, for instance, by limiting heavy machinery in
sensitive areas and using eco-friendly materials
• habitat restoration – habitat restoration measures are
implemented after the completion of construction work to
promote the recovery of biodiversity and reduce long-term
damage to ecosystems; following construction or maintenance
work on transmission line routes, habitat restoration measures
are carried out, such as the restoration of native plant species
and green space rehabilitation
• monitoring and surveillance – regular environmental monitoring
is carried out to assess the degree of impact and make any
necessary adjustments; transmission line maintenance work is
planned and implemented in compliance with seasonal
limitations
The role of Sadales tīkls AS in protecting the white stork is also
important, as approximately 80% or more than 7,300 white stork
nests in Latvia are located on power line poles. To ensure the
safety of birds, the company supports and implements measures
to maintain the white stork population in Latvia.
Prosperity of local communities
Latvenergo Group recognises that the involvement, well-being and
mutual cooperation of local communities is a significant
prerequisite for strengthening public trust and the responsible
development of energy infrastructure. Therefore, the Group
ensures:
• involvement in decision-making – the planning process for new
renewable energy projects involves dialogue with local
communities, listening to their opinions and interests, and
dispelling myths and concerns about the environmental and
human impacts of renewable energy
• safe operation of WPPs for people – at the design stage of wind
power plants, the Group carries out modelling and assessment
to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements and EU
guidelines regarding potential physical impacts, including risks
related to noise (low-frequency noise as well), vibration and
flicker

• support for the local economy – the Group promotes the
involvement of local suppliers and service providers, thereby
creating
job
opportunities,
strengthening
regional
entrepreneurship and fostering economic activity
Education and raising public awareness
The Group implements a range of educational programmes and
awareness campaigns to enhance public understanding of
sustainable lifestyle practices, the importance of biodiversity, and
opportunities for its preservation – fostering societal support for
environmental protection initiatives.
The Group also actively involves its employees and their families
in environmental protection activities. An example of this is the fish
spawning nest project, which has been implemented for 15 years
in collaboration with the “We Are for Fish” association. As a result,
5,610 spawning nests have been placed in the Daugava River.
During the spring 2025 campaign, 450 spawning nests were made
with the participation of Latvenergo Group employees and their
families. This approach not only promotes practical environmental
protection but also provides for an educational experience and
active participation in nature conservation.
The Group's public education programme includes:
• live broadcasts from underwater cameras for observing
spawning and live broadcasts from a white stork nest
• regular expert commentaries on natural processes
• creation of interactive tools to showcase biodiversity activities
• educational events and outdoor excursions
Stakeholder engagement
The Group promotes voluntary initiatives and collaboration with
non-governmental organisations, environmental institutions and
experts to develop effective biodiversity conservation strategies
and foster knowledge exchange. The Group maintains cooperation
with various partners in the field of nature protection and research,
including:
• the Institute of Food Safety, Animal Health and Environment
“BIOR” in the field of fish research
• the University of Latvia and the Latvian and Lithuanian
Ornithological Societies on bird research and protection issues
• nature experts and biologists on monitoring and research
issues
• the Latvian and Lithuanian Nature Conservation Agencies on
natural resource protection issues

Participation in international organisations
Latvenergo is a member of several international organisations and
actively participates in working groups, including WindEurope
working groups – Sustainability, Electrification and Communication
Strategy, which are concerned with biodiversity – promoting the
exchange of experience with other energy companies,
participating in the improvement of EU regulatory frameworks and
applying best practices within Latvenergo projects. Best practice
examples are acquired in the working groups on the use of
solutions inclusive of or complementary to biodiversity during the
design stage and operation of WPPs. Likewise, an essential role is
given to the involvement and education of local communities.
To effectively reduce impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems,
Latvenergo Group adheres to the mitigation hierarchy, which
defines a sequential and targeted set of actions, starting with
solutions that provide the greatest benefit to biodiversity:
1.

the Group, to the extent possible, avoids project development
in areas of high biodiversity and does not permit activities that
may cause significant negative impacts on biodiversity and
ecosystems

2. if avoidance is not feasible, the Group implements preventive
and technical measures to mitigate the potential negative
impact during its project planning, construction and operation
3. if an impact cannot be fully prevented or mitigated, the Group
implements compensatory measures to balance the impact on
biodiversity and ecosystems and ensure that the overall status
of biodiversity does not deteriorate in the long term
4. if an impact on ecosystems or biodiversity is unavoidable, the
Group undertakes restoration measures to rehabilitate the
affected areas and habitats
The Group implements both voluntary and regulatory
environmental mitigation measures, along with additional nature
protection initiatives, to balance impacts and ensure the
sustainability and restoration of ecosystems.
The Group plans its activities based on its historical experience in
nature conservation and on cooperation with scientific institutions
and experts, local nature researchers, local communities and
public organisations. Projects are implemented taking the specific
nature of local ecosystems and historical development into
account. Local knowledge is integrated through collaboration with
local experts and researchers on the specifics of the territories, as
well as by leveraging the experience of local communities in
ecosystem management.

E4-4

Targets
The targets of the Group are closely linked to its impact on biodiversity and ecosystems, as well as to
dependencies, risks and opportunities identified along the value chain. With respect to biodiversity
and ecosystem matters, the Group’s strategy does not establish baseline values or base years; instead,
it defines specific, achievable targets for the coming years. Progress towards the targets’ achievement
is primarily assessed against the predefined target values rather than in comparison to historical
baselines. This approach was chosen as it aligns more effectively with the Group’s strategy. No interim
targets have been established. For information on stakeholder involvement in the target-setting process
of the strategy, please refer to the section General Information. The targets are set voluntarily and:
• reflect the Group’s commitment to reducing negative impact on ecosystems and have been
developed to monitor and assess how the Group's activities affect the natural environment
• help manage the Group’s reliance on ecosystem nature's services and fosters the development of
sustainable practices to ensure the long-term conservation of natural resources
• serve as a tool for risk management by identifying environmental challenges and promoting investment
in environmental restoration and reduction of emissions; at the same time, they open up new
opportunities, such as the development of green technologies, promotion of environmentally friendly
solutions and strengthening of cooperation with stakeholders in the area of sustainable development
In general, the targets serve as a strategic tool that helps integrate biodiversity considerations into the
decision-making processes of the company, thus strengthening its sustainability along the value chain.
The targets include both quantitative objectives with defined achievement timelines and qualitative
objectives and measures that describe the Group’s strategic approach to the protection and restoration
of biodiversity and ecosystems, as well as to the management of related impacts and risks in areas
where precise quantitative indicators are not applicable. Latvenergo Group constitutes the framework
for setting the targets. The sections About the Group and Operating Segments provide information on
the geographical scope of Latvenergo Group’s economic activities and its main operational sites. The
targets mainly relate to the Group’s own operations and include some elements of the upstream and
downstream value chain. Biodiversity compensation measures have not been used in setting targets.
The setting of targets and their achievement have not been verified by an external verifier.
Latvenergo Group’s biodiversity protection measures are planned and implemented in accordance with
the internationally recognised mitigation hierarchy principle. Based on this approach, Latvenergo Group
has set four commitments in the area of biodiversity and ecosystem protection. These commitments have
been included and approved within the framework of the Sustainability Strategy of Latvenergo Group for
2024–2026, thus strengthening the Group’s long-term commitment to nature conservation.
The methodologies used in setting the goals are grounded in the Group’s long-term collaboration with
scientific institutions and experts. The target of improving the ecological quality of habitats is based
on the annual survey and monitoring data from the BIOR Institute on river ecosystem quality. The target
of enhancing the status of fish species and habitats is informed by the BIOR Institute’s 2020–2023
scientific studies on the dynamics of migratory fish populations in the Daugava River basin and the
assessment of fish migration opportunities. The target or the ratio of planted to felled trees is derived
from studies on the effectiveness of forest restoration and regulatory requirements for developing
WPPs. The methodology for assessing impacts on protected areas relies on the latest scientific
research on the dynamics and distribution of protected species populations, ensuring a scientifically
robust approach to impact assessment and the planning of protection measures.

Although the Group’s Sustainability Strategy for 2024–2026 does

Semi-annual assessments are conducted for each target, allowing for

plans. This approach ensures flexible and effective goal tracking while
maintaining a focus on achieving the final outcomes.

The Sustainability Strategy of Latvenergo does not explicitly use
the concept of ecological thresholds as a determining factor in
defining targets. However, the approach is based on scientific
knowledge and international guidelines to ensure that the Group’s
activities do not exceed critical limits, which could cause
irreversible damage to ecosystems.
In addition to specific environmental thresholds related to specific
facilities, impact type, geographical context and characteristics of the
ecosystem, the Group also adheres to general environmental
principles that apply to sustainable operations at the level of the Group:
• conservation of biodiversity by preventing the loss of species
and habitats in territories managed by the Group, wherever

At the planning and coordination level, the environmental
management department of Latvenergo AS is responsible for
determining, observing and monitoring environmental thresholds.
The department is developing procedures; monitoring and drafting
reports on environmental impacts; coordinating with external
partners, including experts, regulators and local communities;
identifying environmental risks, ensuring their integration into the
overall risk management system of the Group; and assessing
potential violations and their impact on the Group’s operations.
At the operational level, production and technical units ensure
compliance with established environmental thresholds on a daily

basis, for instance, by maintaining adequate water levels at HPPs,
monitoring emissions and water quality, and implementing
preventive measures to mitigate environmental impacts. Engineers
and technical personnel ensure accurate measurements and
record-keeping to monitor ecological
thresholds and react
promptly to any deviations from acceptable values.
External monitoring and the role of stakeholders include national
monitoring bodies, among them the National Environmental Service,
which carry out regular inspections and audits to verify compliance
with regulatory thresholds. Local communities and nongovernmental organisations are involved in providing suggestions
and monitoring the ecosystem impacts of the company.
The Group implements a structured and targeted approach to
biodiversity conservation and restoration in compliance with
international environmental standards and EU initiatives, including
the UN Kunming-Montreal Framework and SDGs, the European
Green Deal, and the objectives of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for
2030. The Group’s strategy includes measures to protect and
restore ecosystems, ensure sustainable management of water
resources and reduce direct GHG emissions, which complies with
the EU strategy. These initiatives are implemented in accordance
with science-based approaches and are regularly evaluated to
ensure their effectiveness. Moreover, the Group has developed a
detailed biodiversity transition plan for 2026–2028, which sets out
activities, objectives, measures and their monitoring down to the
level of object groups, ensuring alignment with the abovementioned international and EU initiatives. The Group operates in
compliance with national legislation and regulatory documents on
protected areas, sustainable management of water resources, and
improvement of environmental quality by integrating these aspects
into its business processes.

Sites in protected areas and areas of high biodiversity value and material impacts on biodiversity

The distance of Latvenergo Group’s production facilities to protected areas

In the reporting year, the activities of Latvenergo Group (operation of power lines, production facilities
and construction of new facilities) did not result in material impacts on protected areas.

Type of site and area occupied by
its technological infrastructure

Overhead and cable power lines located in protected areas or micro-reserves stretch for more than
6,800 km and cover an area of 4.9 ha. The data is obtained through geospatial analysis using publicly
available GIS (Geographic Information Systems) data on protected areas (PAs) and species and habitat
micro-reserves. This analysis enables precise area calculations, as accurate data with geographic
coordinates on the location of PAs and power lines is readily accessible. The construction and
maintenance of power lines is carried out by Sadales tīkls AS in compliance with the laws and
regulations governing the protection and use of protected nature areas, ensuring the preservation of
nature and preventing a negative impact on these territories. In forest areas, only potentially dangerous
trees in the overhead power line protection zone, which is outside the power line route, are felled.
Overhead power lines are gradually being converted into underground cable lines, reducing the width
of the power line route and the protective zone and its impact on the landscape and wildlife. Overhead
power lines are rebuilt using insulated conductors and overhead suspension cables.
Other Latvenergo Group facilities, as well as sites of planned activities that are owned or leased by the
Group, or sites where development rights have been acquired by the Group, are located outside areas
with high biodiversity value. BESS are situated within existing infrastructure areas and do not cause
additional impacts on biodiversity beyond these facilities. Although the Group does not have a
significant impact on protected areas, information has been compiled on the distances between
generation facilities and these areas, enabling the identification of assets with potentially higher impact.
Distances to the nearest protected areas have been determined using geospatial data analysis.
Wind farms often require land adaptation, including land-use change and deforestation, which can
impact the environment and biodiversity. No change of land use is required for the construction of
solar parks. Solar parks are built on industrial, agricultural or degraded land. In this context, the Group
is aware of the need to collect and analyse data on land use change and related processes, including
deforestation, in order to ensure a transparent and responsible approach to land development. All landuse change activities have been carried out in compliance with the current legislation and
environmental protection requirements. The construction of solar and wind farms can affect the spatial
configuration of the landscape, including habitat fragmentation and ecosystem connectivity. The
extent of this impact depends on the scale and location of the project and the ecosystem type on the
site of the project. To reduce the potential impact, less sensitive areas are selected, biological corridors
are preserved, landscape integration solutions are used, and compensatory measures are
implemented to restore biodiversity. The impact of planned activities on landscape structure and
ecosystem connectivity is assessed during the initial project evaluation process, using various
methods such as geospatial analysis tools, satellite imagery, ecological monitoring and field studies.

Latvenergo AS is also aware of the impact of HPPs on river ecosystems, especially on fish migration
processes. A number of measures are being implemented to mitigate these impacts and ensure the
biological connectivity of rivers. Preventive measures include optimising the water level regime during
the spawning season and introducing technical solutions to protect fish. Particular attention is paid to
maintaining shallow water areas in spawning grounds and preserving natural rapid stream areas.
Latvenergo Group continues to invest in improving fish migration infrastructure and introducing new
solutions to ensure the sustainable functioning of river ecosystems. In accordance with the Group’s
Action Plan for Migration and Natural Reproduction of Anadromous Fish of the Daugava River Basin,
several research projects have been implemented in recent years; in collaboration with experts and
stakeholders, the planning of new solutions to improve migratory fish migration in the Daugava River
basin is ongoing.
The activities of the Group are not directly attributable to the accidental or deliberate introduction of
invasive alien species. At the same time, the Group ensures appropriate measures to limit the spread
of invasive species within its territories, including controlling the spread of species such as
Sosnowsky’s hogweed on Latvenergo Group properties.

E4-6
Financial impacts related to biodiversity and ecosystem protection
Taking into account the Group’s actual impact on biodiversity, the expected financial implications are
mainly related to implementing compensatory and impact-mitigating measures, as well as voluntary
initiatives for the conservation of biodiversity. These expenses include compliance with regulatory
requirements and additional measures to mitigate the impact on protected areas, species and biotopes,
including:
• measures to improve river ecosystems and protect fish populations
• the natural resources tax on water used to generate electricity at the Daugava HPPs, which is partly
earmarked to finance bank reinforcement works at the water reservoirs of the Daugava HPPs

• measures to mitigate or compensate for environmental impacts of developing solar and wind farms
• measures to protect the white stork and other bird species during the operation of power lines
• research projects and collaboration projects with environmental institutions and non-governmental
organisations to develop and implement future biodiversity conservation measures
The total costs for the implementation of biodiversity compensation and impact mitigation measures
are estimated at more than EUR 6 million (the indicators have not been verified by any other external
body; their verification is performed solely by the independent auditor within the scope of a limited
assurance engagement).
In the reporting year, the Group identified a risk related to biodiversity protection requirements –
significant restrictions on planned electricity generation due to biodiversity protection requirements.
Stricter regulatory requirements and nature protection conditions may affect both the pace of
development of new electricity generation projects and the operating regime of existing generation
assets, creating situations where planned electricity generation volumes are not fully achieved.
Compliance with such requirements may cause additional costs related to expanded environmental
monitoring activities, assessment of impacts on biodiversity and the implementation of impact
mitigation measures. In certain cases, operational restrictions may also be imposed on electricity
generation equipment (for example, periodic restriction of wind turbine operation for the protection of
birds and bats), which may reduce electricity generation volumes and consequently affect the Group’s
revenues. In the long term, these factors may affect the economic return of projects, the predictability
of cash flows and the conditions for attracting financing. They may also create the need for additional
investment in the conservation of biodiversity and ecosystem protection measures.
The Group continues to develop its approach to assessing the financial impacts related to the
protection of biodiversity and ecosystems. The quantification of these impacts will be progressively
expanded as methodologies improve and the quality and availability of data increase.
Critical assumptions and uncertainties relate to a number of factors affecting the HPPs, as well as the
operation of WPPs and SPPs. Regulatory assumptions include a trend towards stronger environmental
protection and biodiversity conservation, which can lead to additional costs and operational
constraints in the energy sector. Uncertainty is mainly related to how regulations will be implemented
in practice and what specific requirements may be applied to hydropower, wind and solar energy
projects. This may complicate the accurate forecasting of potential costs and impacts on the Group’s
operations. Additional uncertainty is related to possible biodiversity protection measures, such as
additional requirements regarding the restoration of ecosystems and habitats, which may increase the
amount of investment required and extend project implementation time frames.
The impact of climate change on biodiversity and ecosystem functions is a significant source of
uncertainty. Due to climate change, precipitation patterns, water levels and river flow may change,
which in turn affects the electricity generation potential of hydropower plants and the status of river
ecosystems. Thus, climate change creates additional uncertainty regarding the future availability of
hydropower resources and how this will affect biodiversity. Similarly, climate change may affect the
availability of wind and solar energy resources by altering wind speed and solar radiation intensity,
which may affect the production efficiency of these energy sources and, accordingly, the Group’s
income.
Overall, these critical assumptions and sources of uncertainty related to the protection of biodiversity
may cause significant challenges that must be considered in future financial impact calculations.
Maintaining the Group’s sustainability and ensuring compliance with environmental regulations
requires adapting to new rules, introducing new technological solutions, and further investing in
biodiversity and ecosystem protection measures.

E5-1

Policies
Latvenego Group policy foresees a transition towards sustainable
production and consumption, ensuring continuous improvement of
environmental and energy efficiency performance in each
business unit. The Group actively pursues resource efficiency and
implements the principles of the circular economy, evaluating the
consumption of services and products, both provided and
received, and ensuring that their life cycle is as long as possible.
Particular attention is given to compliance with the waste hierarchy,
prioritising the prevention of waste generation and the reduction
of resource consumption, as well as ensuring that reuse,
repairability, recycling and recovery are assessed prior to the
application of waste treatment solutions. In cases of unavoidable
waste, appropriate management is ensured by evaluating

ST Shortterm

MT Mediumterm

LT Longterm

recycling and other circular solutions in order to reduce resource
losses and maximise material circularity. This approach is
integrated into resource consumption-related processes, planning,
procurement and cooperation with supply chain partners, ensuring
that circular economy principles are applied across different
stages of resource use and waste management.
Latvenergo Group has implemented a number of complementary
policies that cover key aspects of resource management and the
circular economy, both in the operations of the companies of the
Group and in the most important upstream and downstream parts of
the value chain. Information on the most senior level of management
responsible for the implementation of the policy, as well as a
description of how the interests of key stakeholders have been taken
into account in the policy development process, is provided in the
section General Information under Sustainability Management.

In addition to the policies mentioned in the section General
Information and the third-party standards and initiatives followed
in their development, the use of resources and circular economy
management are addressed by the following regulatory
documents of Latvenergo Group:
• The Environmental and Energy Management Policy, the main
priorities of which include introducing the principles of the
circular economy, improving energy efficiency, and involving
employees and the public in environmental issues
• The Suppliers Code of Conduct, which sets out the basic
principles and expectations the Group has of its suppliers in
terms of the responsible use of resources
For a summary of Latvenergo’s policies on resource use and circular
economy (IROs) management, see Policies adopted to manage material
sustainability matters in the section General Information.
In implementing its policies, the Group complies with relevant third-party
standards and initiatives related to the application of circular economy
principles. The Group has developed internal guidelines for sustainable
procurement, which are based on national and EU regulatory
requirements, green procurement principles and the requirements of the
ISO 14001 environmental management system, as well as taking into
account the requirements of the Waste Framework Directive.
The policies of the Latvenergo Group provide for the sustainable use of
resources, optimization of technological processes, selection of
environmentally friendly materials, and reduction of environmental
impact. To support the transition from the use of primary resources to
secondary (recycled) resources, the policies of the Latvenergo Group
provide for the implementation of principles for waste recycling and
resource reuse, thereby contributing to a reduction in the consumption
of primary materials. Within the framework of the policies, directions are
defined to reduce waste and increase the share of recycling in the
Group’s operations, as well as an expectation that suppliers apply these
principles.
The policies of the Group take into account the IROs in relation to
suppliers, business partners and customers, with the aim of
ensuring that Latvenergo Group:
• identifies and assesses the impacts of resource use –
systematic monitoring and analysis of resource consumption
and waste generation is being implemented
• manages and controls material IROs – measurable targets are
set to improve the efficiency of resources and the continuous
shift towards the principles of the circular economy
• promotes decarbonisation – specific targets are set for increasing
renewable generation capacity and the use of sustainable biomass
In an upstream value chain, based on the Suppliers Code of Conduct,
the Group expects its suppliers to responsibly and efficiently
manage the use of resources, including the reduction of resource

consumption, promotion of longer product and material life cycles,
waste reduction, waste sorting, proper management, reuse or
recycling, and the use of environmentally friendly materials and
technologies. In addition, the Group has implemented a supplier
evaluation and selection policy that includes environmental criteria
to ensure sustainable supply. Furthermore, the Group has developed
the sustainable procurement guidelines, which give preference to
environmentally friendly products and services.
In the downstream value chain, the policies aims to improve
resource use efficiency while reducing the risks of environmental
pollution and resource depletion, as well as promoting the
implementation of circular economy principles. It includes
measures to promote public education on energy efficiency and
sustainable solutions, thereby fostering responsible resource
consumption. The policy also provides for the implementation of
disposal, and recycling programmes for end-of-life equipment,
ensuring their responsible management throughout the entire
lifecycle. In addition, it emphasizes cooperation with waste
management companies to ensure the effective recycling and
recovery of production by-products and waste.
The implementation and effectiveness of resource use and circular
economy policies are monitored within the framework of an integrated
management system, covering resource consumption, the use of
secondary resources, and waste management. Progress is assessed
using data on resource and material accounting, indicators related to
waste volumes and their management, generation and operational
data, and information on measures that reduce consumption,
decrease waste generation, or extend the life cycle of products.
Supervision is conducted regularly at the day-to-day operational level,
through periodic internal inspections and management reports, and
within the framework of internal and external audits. Structural units
heads and environmental management specialists are responsible for
the supervision process within the framework of their competences
and division of responsibilities, ensuring data quality, timely
identification of deviations and implementation of corrective
measures, while senior management evaluates the results and
makes decisions on improving policies.
E5-2

Actions and resources
Latvenergo Group invests in improving resource efficiency,
cooperates with partners and implements initiatives to promote the
use of resources and introduce the principles of the circular economy.
The activities implemented by the Group to optimise resource use and
to apply circular economy principles are carried out as a continuous
process without a defined end date. These activities are integrated

into the Group’s operational activities and long-term development
planning, ensuring their consistent application across all levels of
operations. The activities are primarily carried out using the Group’s
existing resources, including employee competencies, internal
processes and management systems, as well as available
technological solutions and data. Accordingly, the implementation of
these activities is embedded in the Group’s day-to-day operations and
does not require the allocation of significant additional financial or
material resources. Targets and results of actions related to resource
use and the circular economy cover both the Group's operations and
upstream value chain, as outlined in the section Targets.
Resource efficiency
Resource efficiency in the Group’s operations is assessed by
analysing the circulation and use of material resources, including
primary resources – energy resources, materials and equipment –
throughout their lifecycle, with particular emphasis on the efficient use
of resources and the prevention of resource losses. Latvenergo Group
promotes the efficient use of energy resources as part of optimising the
use of primary resources by recording and analysing the flow of energy
consumption, identifying the essential energy consumption for ensuring
production and economic processes and implementing measures to
reduce energy consumption. The Group has a balanced generation
portfolio, consisting mostly of HPPs and highly efficient CHPPs. The
efficiency of energy use in CHPPs is significantly influenced by the
selected operating mode: cogeneration – both heat and electricity are
produced simultaneously; condensation – only electricity is produced.
Operating CHPPs in cogeneration mode allows for the most
efficient use of fuel and significantly reduces the emissions per
unit of energy produced. Using cogeneration potential, CHPP-1
saved 20% of primary energy resources in the reporting year, and
the savings of CHPP-2 amounted to 17%. Furthermore, the thermal
storage system at CHPP-2, constructed in 2021, enables the
accumulation of thermal energy generated in cogeneration mode
and optimises the adjustment of the CHPP operating modes to the
changing market conditions and to cover peak loads. In 2025, the
system delivered primary energy savings of 1.4 GWh.
The energy management system implemented at the companies of
the Group promotes the efficient use of energy resources. To
minimise the waste of energy, Latvenergo AS and
Liepājas enerģija SIA have implemented an energy management
system, while the principles of energy management of Sadales tīkls AS
have been integrated into the environmental management system. In
accordance with the principles of energy management, energy
efficiency indicators have been developed, baseline economic energy
consumption has been established and changes in energy
consumption compared to baseline consumption are analysed.

=== pdf p.147 ===
Recycled resources
The increased use of secondary raw materials is closely related to
the implementation of circular economy practices. Secondary raw
materials can only be obtained when waste is properly collected,
sorted, and returned to production processes instead of being
disposed of. By introducing separate waste collection and
management in the Group’s capital companies, and by concluding
contracts with waste management systems that follow circular
economy principles, waste can be recovered and processed into
secondary raw materials. These measures support the increased
availability and use of secondary raw materials. In addition, in
implementing its procurement policy, the Group promotes the use
of secondary materials and recycled resources where this is
technically and economically feasible. The developed sustainable
procurement guidelines support the practical integration of circular
economy principles into day-to-day operations.
Sustainable consumption
The operations of Latvenergo Group are characterised by a
number of circular business practices related to the sustainable
use of resources and waste management.
Latvenergo Group systematically implements a number of value
conservation initiatives aimed at the sustainable use of resources.
The Group regularly maintains and repairs equipment and
infrastructure to extend the life of assets. Maintenance and
upgrading of production plant equipment is also carried out along
with the renewal of existing infrastructure elements. Particular
attention is paid to technology upgrades aimed at improving plant
efficiency and reducing emissions.
In the area of value development, the Group actively promotes more
extensive use of energy efficiency solutions, which maximises value
for consumers. Important projects, such as the development of the
electricity charging network, are being carried out in close
cooperation with local authorities and other organisations to ensure
greater access to infrastructure. Work is also underway on
expanding the use of RES and initiatives aimed at reducing CO2
emissions. In addition, the Group actively supports local
communities and Ukrainian aid initiatives by donating recyclable
materials. Such measures promote compliance with the principles of
the circular economy, strengthen cooperation with community
members and contribute to sustainable resource management.
End-of-life activities include the recycling and reuse of endof- life
equipment and components in the industry. The same approach is
also expected from suppliers and business partners. All types of
waste, including hazardous waste, are managed in strict

compliance with laws and regulations and the principles of
sustainable development.
The Group uses the principles of industrial symbiosis in cooperation
with other companies to promote system efficiency. For instance,
the ash from energy production is sold for agricultural use to
improve the land. The Group does not track the physical quantities
of individual raw materials across the entire supply chain; however,
it actively collaborates with suppliers and partners through ongoing
engagement, including information exchange, joint discussions on
compliance requirements and the provision of advisory support
where improvements are needed. These activities are aimed at
ensuring a high level of transparency and traceability of resources,
especially in the solar panel supply chain.
In the area of circular economy and resource use, the Latvenergo
Group carries out significant cooperation across the value chain,
based on bilateral cooperation models with stakeholders. The
Group cooperates with suppliers, service providers, equipment
manufacturers and waste management systems to promote the
sustainable sourcing of raw materials, material traceability and
compliance with waste management requirements. The approach
applies to materials and equipment components used in energy
production and infrastructure maintenance, as well as components
of renewable energy equipment. The cooperation structure ensures
the implementation of circular economy principles with clearly
defined roles across the upstream and downstream value chain.

• by-product reuse – the use of ash from production to improve
land, thus preventing it from becoming waste and promoting
industrial symbiosis
The Group’s focus on sustainable energy production and efficient
management of materials contributes to optimising waste
management and reducing environmental pressures.
Implementing these measures ensure a consistent contribution to
achieving the objectives of Latvenergo Group’s resource use and
circular economy policies, while supporting their integration into the
Group’s strategic planning and day-to-day operations. Investments
in improving energy efficiency – including the operation of CHPs in
cogeneration mode, the implementation of heat accumulation
solutions, and the maintenance of energy management systems –
directly support the policy objective of reducing primary resource
consumption and increasing the efficiency of energy production
throughout the entire life cycle of assets. The use of sustainable
biomass, the integration of secondary resources, and waste
prevention measures contribute to the implementation of circular
economy principles and to keeping materials in circulation. To
enhance the efficiency of material flows, the Group implements
solutions for the reuse of resources, while simultaneously
integrating sustainability requirements into supply chain
management, thereby strengthening circular principles both within
the Group and across its supplier network.

Waste management

E5-3

The operations of Latvenergo Group include a number of strategic
elements that contribute to preventing waste creation in both the
upstream and downstream value chain. These elements include
sustainable use of resources, careful selection of suppliers,
application of industrial symbiosis principles and implementation
of energy-efficient solutions:

Targets

• use of sustainable resources – Liepājas enerģija SIA uses
sustainable biomass fuels that meet the criteria for saving GHG
emissions, thus contributing to waste minimisation at the
resource extraction stage
• careful selection of suppliers – sustainability requirements,
including responsible sourcing and production, are taken into
account in the selection process for suppliers. This approach
helps reduce negative environmental impacts and prevents the
development of waste
• procurement planning for materials and equipment – Latvenergo
Group carefully plans its procurement of materials and
equipment to avoid overstocking or build-up of unused materials

Latvenergo Group strives for sustainable production and
consumption. It promotes continuous improvement of the
environmental and energy performance of each business unit,
pursuing the efficient use of resources and the implementation of
circular economy principles. The consumption of services and
products provided and received is evaluated and the life cycle of
products is maintained as long as possible. A strong focus is
placed on waste prevention and reduction, ensuring appropriate
waste management, as well as evaluating the possibilities of reuse,
regeneration and recycling.
Waste management objectives have been set taking into account
the requirements of the EU Waste Framework Directive
(2008/98/EC) and the waste management hierarchy, national
waste management objectives, the Group’s Sustainability Strategy,
as well as the local context and available infrastructure.

Latvenergo Group constitutes the framework for setting the targets. The sections About the Group and
Operating Segments provide information on the geographical scope of Latvenergo Group’s economic
activities and its main operational sites. The Latvenergo Group’s resource use and circular economy
objectives primarily apply to the Group’s directly managed generation, grid and resource management
activities, while also integrating the most significant value chain aspects – the sustainable supply of
biomass, the recycling of equipment and materials, as well as cooperation with suppliers to promote
innovation and the use of local resources. The targets are set on a voluntary basis, using a
methodology that considers the current situation, the feasibility of technical and economic solutions,
the capacity of existing waste management infrastructure, and examples of best practices within the
sector. While industry guidelines and available research are taken into account, a detailed scientific
analysis has not been conducted. No interim targets have been established. For information on
stakeholder involvement in the target-setting process of the strategy, please refer to the section
General Information. Progress towards the targets' achievement is primarily assessed against the
predefined target values rather than in comparison to historical baselines. This approach was chosen
as it aligns more effectively with the Group’s strategy and allows for greater flexibility in responding to
developments within the energy sector. Progress is regularly reviewed and, if necessary, updated in
line with changes in regulatory frameworks and the development of the Group's operations.
Latvenergo Group’s commitments in the area of the circular economy and performance in the reporting year:
• use of sustainable biomass – Liepājas enerģija SIA uses a biomass fuel – wood – at its production
sites. Over the reporting year, 100% of biomass fuels used met the criteria for sustainability and
saving GHG emissions, ensuring compliance with the requirements of the regulatory enactments
of the European Union and the Republic of Latvia. Traceability of biomass is ensured throughout
the supply chain. Biomass extraction is based on the principles of sustainable forestry, thus
ensuring the conservation of biodiversity and reforestation
• measures to promote sustainable consumption – Latvenergo Group implemented more than ten
measures to promote sustainable consumption in the reporting year

E5-4

Resource inflows
The resources essential for Latvenergo Group’s operations are
those related to power generation, electricity distribution and
infrastructure maintenance. These resources are fundamental to
ensuring the continuity and quality of the Group’s operations and
account for the majority of the Group’s incoming resource flows.
In addition to these main resource flows, other material flows also
occur in the Group’s operations, including packaging received
together with purchased goods. As at the reporting date, data on
these flows are not sufficiently complete to allow for quantitative
disclosure. Taking into account the limitations in data availability
and the relatively low significance of these flows, they are
therefore not included in the quantitative reporting of incoming
resource flows..
Energy distribution infrastructure components
The operations of Sadales tīkls AS focus on the maintenance,
upgrading and provision of reliable energy supply to customers.
To support these activities, the company uses a number of key
input resources: wires and cables, transformers, substation
equipment, poles and supports for overhead lines, electrical
metering equipment and technological resources.
Materials and resources related to RES projects
The companies of the Group are actively pursuing the construction
of SPPs and WPPs, thus promoting the use of RES and the
development of sustainable energy production.
Based on the IROs identified in the double materiality assessment,
the Latvenergo Group identifies, as a significant resource inflow,
the resources required for the development of new renewable
energy assets and energy storage technologies.
These resource flows include core equipment such as solar panels,
inverters, wind turbines and tower structures, as well as BESS

During the reporting year, the Latvenergo Group initiated the
identification and quantification of incoming resource flows,
focusing on renewable energy assets commissioned in 2025
within its own operations – SPPs, WPPs and BESS. The current
assessment of incoming resources covers the most significant
core equipment and key structural components. Data on the
physical volumes of auxiliary equipment and construction-related
materials are not included in this reporting period.
The collection of comprehensive and fully comparable information
on the physical mass of materials across all renewable energy
projects is constrained by the nature of project implementation, as
these are executed as complex CapEx projects with fragmented
procurement processes and multiple contracting stages, including
the use of subcontractors.
During the reporting period, the Latvenergo Group had not
implemented a centralised system for tracking physical material
flows at the project level, and accounting is primarily based on
financial data. Consequently, the disclosed data reflect an initial
stage of assessing incoming resources and are partly based on
estimates.
Despite the above limitations, during the reporting year the
Latvenergo Group made reasonable efforts to compile quantitative
information on incoming resources in renewable energy assets,
including:
• the development of internal procedures for tracking flows of
solar panels, inverters and batteries, as well as for the
management of end-of-life equipment
• a detailed analysis of the material composition of solar panels
• the initiation of mapping of key incoming resource categories
across newly constructed SPPs, WPPs and BESS projects
• a review of available procurement documentation and
technical specifications, including requests for information
from key equipment manufacturers and suppliers
• the initiation of the development of an internal methodology for
the structured collection of data on material flows

=== pdf p.150 ===
The development of renewable energy and energy storage technologies increases the Group’s
dependence on certain raw materials, including EU Critical Raw Materials, the limited availability and
concentrated supply chains of which may lead to supply disruptions and price volatility. At the same
time, enhancing the resilience of renewable energy technologies to climate change impacts and
promoting the use of durable, repairable and recyclable equipment can reduce resource losses and
waste generation, while strengthening the Group’s long-term operational resilience.
The inflows of resources related to RES assets were quantified using a material mass and material
composition approach. The objective of the calculation was to identify and assess the total mass of
materials entering the Group’s value chain in the context of asset construction, installation, and
refurbishment, while also evaluating the quality and reliability of the data used. The mass of incoming
resources was determined in tonnes, applying a combined methodology. Where unit weights and
quantities of equipment or components were available, total mass was calculated by multiplying unit
weight by the number of units. For structural elements, mass was determined based on documented
construction volumes and material densities. In cases where only installed capacity was known,
industry-average mass indicators per unit of installed capacity were applied. Material composition was
identified based on manufacturers’ technical documentation and material safety data sheets. Where
manufacturer-specific documentation was not directly available, estimates of material mass and
composition were based on publicly available industry sources, including data on typical material
composition of solar and wind energy equipment, as well as publicly available technical specifications
from manufacturers. Where such information was also unavailable, a functional analysis of
components was applied.
The reported indicators on resource inflows are predominantly based on primary data obtained from
the Group’s internal systems and project documentation, complemented by secondary data and
estimates where direct measurements are not available. Based on the assessment of resource inflows
by mass, as well as the quality and structure of the underlying data, approximately 18% of the total
volume is based on directly measured data and documented quantities. Approximately 17% is derived
using refined estimates, including cases where detailed technical information – such as material
composition or specifications – is available, but material mass is calculated indirectly. A further 54%
of the assessment of resource inflows is based on estimates, primarily where detailed measurement
data is unavailable and secondary data sources or standardised indicators are used. The remaining
11% is based on assumptions, particularly where information on the weight of specific equipment or
materials was not available at the time of reporting.
The classification of material criticality and hazardousness has been carried out in accordance with the
European Union Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) and the REACH Regulation (EC) No
1907/2006. These regulatory frameworks are used for classification and disclosure purposes and do not
directly affect the calculated material mass. Identified data gaps have been documented, and opportunities
to progressively improve data availability and accuracy will be assessed in future reporting periods.
At present, the Group is not able to provide quantitative information on circularity in line with ESRS
E5- 4 requirements, due to the lack of sufficiently reliable data on the volumes of recycled or reused
materials and their share in total resource consumption. In addition, the necessary data collection
processes and methodological approach for assessing circular material flows have not yet been fully
developed and implemented.
During 2026, the Group plans to finalise the development of its methodology for tracking material flows.
This will enable an expanded scope of incoming resources in future reporting periods, improved data
quality and comparability, as well as the systematic collection of information on the share of recycled
and reused materials, thereby strengthening the integration of circular economy principles in the
development of renewable energy projects.

During the reporting year, the total mass of key equipment inflows for the construction of new RES
assets exceeded 155 thousand tonnes. The largest share is attributable to WPPs projects, while the
mass of SPPs panels represents a significant, but comparatively smaller portion, and BESS account
for a relatively minor share of the total volume. The analysis indicates that resource inflows are
dominated by steel and concrete, primarily within wind energy infrastructure, whereas glass and
aluminium constitute a substantial share of solar panel composition.
At the same time, the analysis shows that EU CRMs, such as silver used in solar panels and lithium
used in BESS, represent only a very small proportion (0.03%) of the total resource inflow by mass. The
presence of critical raw materials is mainly associated with functional components and battery
chemistry, rather than structural materials.
It should be noted that the Laflora Energy wind farm project in Latvia applies an innovative hybrid
tower design, where the lower tower sections are made of reinforced concrete produced locally in
Latvia by Consolis Latvia SIA, while the upper section of the tower is constructed from steel. The main
constituents of concrete – limestone, sand, cement, and water – are not included in the list of critical
raw materials defined under Regulation (EU) 2024/1252. Compared to fully steel tower structures, this
solution reduces dependency on steel supply chains, while also lowering transport-related emissions
and supporting the development of local industry.

strategy for CHPPs and HPPs provides for the regular refurbishment and repair of key components,
enabling a reduction in the need for new material and equipment procurement, while increasing the
reuse of existing resources and extending their life cycle.

The main products of Latvenergo Group are electricity and thermal energy produced in HPPs and
CHPPs. In addition, the Group offers electricity and natural gas trading, energy efficiency solutions,
electromobility services and other sustainable products in the market of the Baltic states. The
production process generates by-products and waste, which are managed in accordance with the
principles of the circular economy. Latvenergo Group’s priority is to prevent waste from ending up in
landfills, with preference given to recycling, energy recovery or reuse.
The Group has introduced measures and technologies that help reduce waste at the source. Processes
are improved and resource use is optimised to reduce consumption of materials and energy resources,
thus reducing the generation of waste and promoting its reuse.
All waste is thoroughly sorted to ensure maximum reuse and recycling. Latvenergo AS, in compliance
with the principles of environmental protection and sustainability, cooperates with operators that
adhere to extended producer responsibility to ensure recycling and recovery of waste in accordance
with the requirements of the regulatory enactments and not less than to the amounts specified in these
regulatory enactments.
Waste that cannot be recycled or reused is treated and disposed of in a safe and environmentally friendly
way. All safe disposal measures are carried out in cooperation with waste management companies.
Latvenergo AS is also actively involved in changing the waste management habits of society. Since 1997,
the EEC, the only one of its kind in the Baltic states, has been operating under the auspices of Latvenergo
with the purpose of creating public awareness on the efficient use of energy resources, including the
introduction of environmentally friendly solutions and waste management. During the reporting year, the
EEC organised various educational activities, seminars and campaigns, including campaigns aimed at
promoting public involvement in the circular economy and reaching sustainability objectives.
In the reporting year, the management of waste generated by the companies of the Group was
organised according to the principles of the circular economy. Of the total waste generated, 45% was

Classification of waste and recyclable materials
The Group's companies currently do not have detailed accounting of waste material composition.
Waste accounting is carried out in accordance with the requirements of regulatory enactments
according to waste classification codes. The Group is evaluating the possibilities of introducing more
detailed accounting of waste composition in the future.
Data on the amount of waste managed is compiled from invoices issued by waste managers, as well
as waste transportation consignment notes. If necessary, coefficients are used to convert from waste
volume in cubic meters (m3) to weight (tonnes) as specified in the regulation of the Cabinet of Ministers
No. 1075 Regulations on State Statistical Report Forms for Environmental Protection and in the MEPRD
methodological instructions On Filling in Statistical Report No. 3 – Waste. Report on Waste. These
coefficients are regularly.reviewed and updated in accordance with changes in regulatory enactments.
The data are reported at the volume recorded in actual measurements or, where such data are not
available, recalculated using regulatory coefficients; conservative assumptions are applied only in
situations where direct weighing data are not available. Invoices and delivery notes from waste
management operators provide external verification of the accuracy of the quantities transferred for
management, while internal data aggregation and classification are performed within the Group. The
most significant waste accounting data are also reviewed by the independent auditor within the scope
of a limited assurance engagement, providing additional assurance of their compliance.

E5-6
Risks and financial effects from the circular economy and resource use
The materiality assessment of the Group identified one material risk with a potential financial impact.
The risk of critical supply chains is associated with potential disruptions that can lead to increases in
production costs and reduced resource availability. The risk impact assessment uses both internal
information on supply chain stability and external market and industry information on resource
availability and development trends in order to identify possible scenarios and their potential financial
impact. The financial impact of this risk is difficult to quantify in the short term, but in the medium and
long term, it can have a significant impact on the Group’s competitiveness, especially if dependence
on certain suppliers increases or new regulations on imported materials are introduced. To mitigate
this risk, alternative sources of supply are being explored, and the resilience of supply chains is being
improved.
Anticipated financial effects from material opportunities
The Group has identified one material opportunity in the area of resource use and the circular economy,
which has a potential positive financial impact in the medium and longer term.
Improving the sustainability of equipment – investments in increasing the resilience of equipment to
the impacts of climate change will, in the long term, improve asset longevity, significantly reduce
potential financial losses from infrastructure damage, and allow the deferral of necessary investments
in the replacement of depreciated assets. In this context, particular attention is paid to electricity
generation and distribution infrastructure that is exposed to extreme weather events, for instance,
severe storms and floods. Such investments will not only improve the longevity of assets but also
contribute to more stable and predictable financial flows.
Innovative solutions for waste recycling – introduction of new technological solutions for recycling of
solar panels and WPPs components at the end of their life cycle may generate gradual financial
benefits, with increasing potential in the long term. This approach not only reduces management costs
but also generates additional revenue by using recycled materials to manufacture new products.
Furthermore, given the rapid development of the regulation on the circular economy in the European
Union, the Group can benefit from actively participating in the development of relevant regulatory
enactments and adapting its operations to sustainable business models.
The opportunity assessment process uses both internal and external information on technological
development trends, market dynamics and regulatory directions in order to identify their potential
impact on the Group’s efficiency, cost base and revenue potential. A number of critical assumptions
are essential for the successful implementation of the circular economy and resource efficiency
strategy. One of these is a stable and predictable regulatory framework in the waste management
sector, enabling effective planning and long-term investment in sustainable management systems.
The development and availability of recycling technologies is equally crucial, which will contribute to
a moderate to significantly positive impact on cost efficiency by enabling more economically
advantageous reuse of resources.

IROs related to water resources and fuel consumption were

transparency, and contributes to the implementation of
sustainable development principles.

The Group mainly uses water resources for the provision of
production processes and, in small quantities, for other economic
needs and for the water supply to external consumers. The amount
of surface and/or groundwater consumption is specified in the
permits of each facility. Water is the principal resource for
electricity generation in the HPPs. The availability and volume of
this resource depends on natural conditions and seasonal
fluctuations in water levels.
The Group’s water consumption balance includes water from the
surface, groundwater and centralised water supply networks.
Water consumption data is obtained from verified commercial
meters, whose accuracy is regularly checked in accordance with
the requirements of metrological control of measuring instruments.
As the water consumption of CHPPs is mainly influenced by the
operating modes of the production facilities and the amount of
energy generated, the amount of water consumed has increased
as a result of the increase in generation.

Water resources

activities. During the reporting year, these limits were not exceeded.

The management of IROs is integrated into the operating processes of the Group’s companies, and

determination of Latvenergo Group’s material sustainability targets is based on internationally

objectives of the Group and impacts specific to its operations. The setting of targets and their

capital companies’ risk management. At least once a year, the Management Board of Latvenergo AS
submits a report on the Group’s risk management to the Supervisory Board of Latvenergo AS, which
is responsible for overseeing the Group’s risk management system.
The above approach is fully applied to the management of all sustainability issues and targets.

In the reporting year, the number of overtime hours in the Group’s parent company increased by approximately 16% compared
to 2024. In 2025, the number of overtime hours at Sadales tīkls AS decreased by 2.3% compared to 2024. An increase in the
volume of overtime has been recorded in certain structural units and is not systematic. It is mainly related to fluctuations in the
volume of operations, increased project intensity and limitations in resource availability. The Group identifies the increase in
employee workload as a significant work condition risk, which may potentially affect employee well-being, work-life balance and
the long-term sustainability of work capacity. Workload indicators are regularly monitored. Responsible managers are involved
in situations where in-depth analysis or additional management attention is required. To remedy increased employee workload,
the following activities are implemented: flexible work organization, supervision sessions, educational initiatives on work–life
balance, improvements to the working environment, etc.

The Group implements an employee well-being programme, which contains physical, emotional and professional well-being. It
includes individual supervision sessions and personal discussions with HR business partners, as well as a comprehensive
conference programme, providing each employee with the opportunity to choose the most suitable path for professional and
personal development. Significant improvements have been made to the physical work environment at several sites, while the
digital work environment has also been modernised through the implementation of the Microsoft 365 platform. Together, these
improvements form a comprehensive system that supports employee well-being, fosters engagement and strengthens the sense
of belonging to the Group.

Employee commitment and experience study
In 2025, a comprehensive study was conducted, assessing
employee commitment according to the TRI*M methodology and
employee experience through various questions. 2,576
respondents, or 79% of the Group’s total workforce, took part in
the survey.
The commitment indicator is based on the answers the employees
gave to questions about general satisfaction, willingness to
recommend the workplace, willingness to reapply for their job,
motivation of colleagues, and assessment of the company’s
performance and competitiveness.
In the reporting year, the commitment index reached 67 points
(70 points in 2024), which is still higher than the average in Latvia
overall (64 points on average in Latvia in 2025). Similarly, this
index is higher than the overall European employee commitment
index (60 points), as well as the utilities sector index (55 points).
The value is medium-high, indicating a good and stable work
environment.
